APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS OF STAFF BOARD
speechtext:
I should like to make an announcement which will, I know, be of interest to all hon. members.
The house will recall that the sixth report of the special committee on procedure and organization tabled on May 20 outlined a complete reorganization of the staff and services of the House of Commons, as recommended by the Speaker and approved by the commissioners of internal economy. The reorganization provides for the establishment of a three man staff board under the chairmanship of a director of administration. In addition to the new post of director of administration, provision has been made for three other new positions; a director of legislative services, a secretary for parliamentary associations and a second deputy sergeant-at-arms, the latter to be employed on a sessional basis.
I am pleased to inform the house that appointments have now been made to all three new full time positions. The sessional deputy sergeant-at-arms will be selected in the near future.
The position of director of administration will be filled by Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel, who
has been secretary of the civil service commission and, more recently, co-ordinator of language training in the civil service. Mr. Hamel, a native of Quebec city, holds the degrees of bachelor of commerce and master of commerce in business administration from Laval University, Quebec, as well as that of master of public administration from the Maxwell school at Syracuse university, New York. He has had extensive experience in personnel selection, position classification, and public administration generally. As director of administration he will relieve the Clerk of many of his routine signing and approval duties and will be responsible for the work of the various administrative service branches. Personnel and financial control will be among his major responsibilities. Initially Mr. Hamel will be on a one year loan from the commission.
For the position of director of legislative services Mr. Alex Small, the present chief of journals, was unanimously selected as the result of a competition. Mr. Small has had 12 years' experience on the House of Commons staff in three of its branches, committees, index and journals. During world war II Mr. Small served as a navigator in the R.C.A.F. with the rank of flight lieutenant on release. He was mentioned in dispatches and spent a year in a prisoner of war camp in Germany. Prior to joining the House of Commons staff Mr. Small had extensive administrative experience in the Department of National Health and Welfare.
In his new post Mr. Small will direct the work of the committees branch, English and French debates, English and French journals and the English and French index and reference branches. He will also serve as third clerk assistant and have some duties at the table.
The staff board, which will comprise the director of administration, the Sergeant-at-Arms and director of building services, and the director of legislative services, with the chief of personnel, Mr. Len Hill, as its secretary, will commence at once to deal with various outstanding personnel and administrative problems. These include personal grievances as to salary levels, unsatisfactory working conditions, vacation leave, hours of

Appointment of Staff Board work, doubtful hiring practices and so on. Meanwhile a complete classification study of all positions on the House of Commons staff is already under way and should result in salary adjustments wherever warranted.
Provision is also being made for the establishment, for the first time, of a formal grievance procedure so that legitimate employee grievances will be dealt with in a prompt and orderly fashion. Grievances not settled by the immediate supervisor or the director concerned will be considered by the staff board and, if necessary, the Clerk of the house. It is hoped to eliminate the unsatisfactory practice of having employees take their grievances direct to the Speaker or to individual members of parliament.
The position of secretary for parliamentary associations will be filled by Mr. Ian Imrie, presently assistant chief of national historic sites in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Mr. Imrie is an honour graduate in arts of Trinity College, University of Toronto, and has had postgraduate training in Europe. He will devote his attention to co-ordinating the staff services for delegations to the various interparliamentary groups, for example the commonwealth parliamentary association, the Canada-U.S. interparliamentary group, the NATO parliamentary association, the interparliamentary union and special parliamentary visits and exchanges that may be arranged from time to time.
I might just add that while the reorganization also contemplates the appointment of an executive assistant to the Speaker, no action is necessary for the time being. Mr. George Carty, a senior civil servant loaned to me to act as secretary to the special committee on procedure and organization, has been carrying out extra duties on my behalf with the title of special assistant to the Speaker.
I should like to record our indebtedness to the organization division of the civil service commission for their assistance to me in working out this reorganization and, in particular, to Mr. H. L. Laframboise, who at my urgent request carried out a complete study of our organization structure. At my suggestion, and in full co-operation with the parliamentary librarian, Mr. Laframboise is now conducting a study of the library in the hope of improving its service to parliament.
At this time I should also like to express my appreciation of the full support and cooperation of the Clerk of the house in making these important changes. Mr. Raymond, the Sergeant-at-Arms and other senior officers

of the house share my desire to bring our organization structure into line with the altered and vastly increased demands of the present day.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was asked yesterday by the hon. member for Danforth whether I would make a statement in regard to a reply which

I gave toward the end of last Friday's sitting to an oral question from him, which reply has caused some misunderstanding. The question repeated one made by the hon. member himself on May 20 asking for a study of the social, cultural and economic effects on the rest of Canada of separation by Quebec and, to quote him as he is reported at page 3401 of Hansard:
-so the fullest measure of information would be available to discuss this important subject.
I said at that time that I would give consideration to the proposal but that-and I quote from my reply-
-I would like to add that we are convinced any such study would be entirely academic, because no such separation is going to take place.
The hon. member at that time agreed, but he still thought-and I again quote from his remarks in Hansard-

that there are people in Canada who really think Canada can get along separately, and that it might be useful if this type of information were available.
Those were his words. My answer last Friday was given in the framework of that earlier reply-that a study along those lines would be academic but that the information might be useful. At that time, on May 20, no one took any exception to this exchange. Last Friday strong exception was taken to it. I said on Friday that that kind of investigation -they were my words-is being made; but I also indicated quite clearly that it is confined to the economic aspects rather than the broader range suggested by the hon. member for Danforth. I further indicated quite plainly, Mr. Speaker, that it would be a study not of separation but of the economic interrelations within Canada. It would be a study of the indivisibility of our economy, the indivisibility which would be created by the interrelation of the various parts. It will show, I hope and believe, how the parts of Canada need each other.
To say that we should not study the facts on which our unity is based as well as certain pressures on that unity is, I believe, to show unnecessary fear and lack of faith. To say that in making such a study we are contemplating the division of our country is like saying that we must be warmongers if we study the necessity for defence forces. Ours, Mr. Speaker, is an unusual economy. The vastness of its area and the diversity of its resources mean that regional differences are especially important, and therefore economic interrelations are of special significance.
Federal-Provincial Relations
Matters of this kind have already been examined. They were examined in a famous study, "The economic background of dominion-provincial relations" prepared for the Rowell-Sirois commission by one of Canada's most distinguished economists, Dr. W. A. Mackintosh. I do not think anyone would now dispute the value of this study, but it was made a generation ago. Much has changed since, but there has been no equivalent study made.
I believe it is time that the same economic examination is made again in the light, of new conditions. It will be a study of our economic unity within confederation; but because that unity is built not on uniformity but on diversity we have continually to think of ways and means of maintaining and strengthening it. Our national economic policies have to be based on the facts as they exist today and on an understanding of our problems as they have changed.
The study will be of special value in showing the factors which should influence federal-provincial relationships in the economic and financial fields. In this respect it should be of service, and I believe will be of service, to the federal representatives on the tax structure committee which was planned at the Quebec conference and which, it is hoped, will soon begin its work.
Mr. Speaker, to fail to strengthen the forces of unity in our economy would be a dereliction of duty. The one thing which could bring about such disaster as disunity would be for a federal government to bury its head in the sand, to be afraid of the facts and to refuse to study problems; and we will not be guilty of that.
Since some questions have been asked outside the house, I should perhaps conclude with a word about the procedure that is being followed in this matter. It is a perfectly normal procedure. As hon. members know, studies of this kind are not launched suddenly out of the air. They have to be planned. I have therefore asked a few government officials, economic experts, to advise me on what would be involved in a study of the economic interrelations within our country and how such a study could best be made.
Considered answers to these questions involve quite a bit of preliminary work. When that preliminary work has been done, I will then be in a position to make a recommendation to cabinet as to what formal steps may be required to carry through this study in the light of conditions we now face in this country

Federal-Provincial Relations in the economic and financial fields of federal-provincial relations. When the cabinet has made its decision on this matter as a result of the report I hope to be able to make to it, that decision will be conveyed to the house.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard from the Prime Minister; as has happened in the past, a clarifying statement has had to be made as the result of a careless statement made by the government in connection with a policy announcement. I want to say at once that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition is ill with a heavy cold today. I am sure if he had been here he would have commented on the statement that has been made by the Prime Minister with far more emphasis than I can.
However, if we go back over the events that led to this statement of clarification today it will be seen, I am sure, that all of us who were present obtained an entirely different impression; as a matter of fact, even the members of the press did also, as will be seen from newspaper reports. On May 20 the hon. member for Danforth posed a lengthy question, reported on page 3401 of Hansard. Amongst other things he said:
-would the government consider ordering a study of the economic, cultural and social effects upon the rest of Canada of separation by Quebec-
Now, it is quite clear what that question meant. The Prime Minister said in his reply, amongst other things, that any such study would be entirely academic because no such separation is going to take place. This was a good statement by the Prime Minister. However, last Friday the hon. member for Danforth, pursuing the same point, asked again whether the Prime Minister had given any consideration to his previous request of May 20. The Prime Minister replied in these words, as reported at page 4780 of Hansard:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we have been considering the matter. It is not a subject which lends itself to easy investigation and dogmatic conclusions, but officials of the government are making that kind of investigation now.
Anyone reading the original question would come to the conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that this committee of civil servants was making a study of the economic, cultural and social effects upon the rest of Canada of separation by Quebec. It was quite evident that there was a misunderstanding by everybody because the Prime Minister, some four hours later, felt impelled to make a statement of clarification as to what he actually meant by his reference to such a study. Anyone listening to the Prime Minister at that time would

have come to the conclusion that this government was studying the effects of separation by Quebec from the rest of Canada. This was indeed a strange attitude to be taken by any government, since they should have been studying measures to bring about unity in Canada rather than separation.
Yesterday the hon. member for Danforth referred to what he called an irresponsible statement by the Leader of the Opposition which was issued to the press late Friday afternoon. I say, in view of this whole situation, the irresponsible statements that have been made prior to today have been made by the Prime Minister of this country and the government he represents.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the members of this party are fully in support of the type of study which the Prime Minister has outlined. To suggest that any such study is an endorsation of the idea of separatism seems to me politically irresponsible-

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Not in the original terms.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
-and can only pander to those parts of Canada which are seeking to exploit the differences that may exist between English speaking and French speaking Canada. The members of this house cannot bury their heads in the sand like ostriches. The fact is that talk of separatism is prevalent. I do not think there are many members in this house and I doubt that there are many people in Canada who are in favour of separatism. The fact is, however, that the idea is promulgated. Economic and constitutional arguments are being advanced as to the advisability of the province of Quebec becoming an associate state or even a state separate from the rest of Canada. Cognizance of this fact was taken by the Quebec legislature, which has set up a committee to study the whole question.
I have before me the terms of reference of that committee. They are fairly lengthy and

I will not read them, but in summary the committee was asked to study to what extent the province of Quebec could acquire greater constitutional authority without destroying its own economic viability. This study is to look into whether Quebec is putting more into confederation than it is getting out of it, and whether it would be to its advantage to seek a separate status from the rest of Canada.
I do not take this to mean that the legislature of Quebec is anxious to promote separatism. I take this to mean that they are seeking to gather the data upon which they can answer the arguments that are being advanced in some parts of Canada. When that study is completed it will certainly be used in the province of Quebec and elsewhere to argue for certain transfers of constitutional, monetary and fiscal authority from the federal government to the provinces.
It seems to me that in the light of that fact, Mr. Speaker, the government of Canada and the members of this house need to be armed with all the information they can get. We are not going to answer the arguments of the separatists by putting our heads in the sand or by thinking that if we keep quiet the problem will go away. Nor are we going to be able to answer by waving the flag and beating our breasts about confederation.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext: What flag?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
In the long run light will do more than heat in dealing with this problem, and the parliament of Canada and the government of Canada need to be armed with all the arguments, all the data and all the economic facts so they can present them to the people of Canada. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, when the government finally decides on the basis for this study I hope the commission will be a fairly strong one, that on it the government will put some able economists who will study not only the problem of separatism but will study also the extent to which the parliament of Canada can continue to strip the federal government of its constitutional powers without destroying the economic viability of Canada as a whole.
Under various pressures concessions have been made. Certain powers have been taken from the federal government and given to the provincial government. I am not going to argue now which of these were wise and which were unwise, but the one thing we do know is that if Canada is to continue as a viable economy there are powers which the
Federal-Provincial Relations government of Canada must retain in order that this country may operate economically and efficiently.
We will only get that kind of information if there is the fullest possible study, not only of the relations of English speaking Canada and French speaking Canada, but of the federal government's economic relations to all the provinces. We are in great danger in Canada of becoming regionalized to the point where the type of economic planning which has become part and parcel of the program of almost every industrial country in the world will be meaningless if we continue to go down a road that, while it might maintain a semblance of unity, would actually lead to the economic disintegration of this country.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker we support the idea of such a study. We hope the government will not leave this to busy government officials who have many other things to do, but that a commission of outstanding economists and constitutional experts will be given this task in order that we may have something similar to the Rowell-Sirois commission that will give Canada a blueprint which we can follow for the next quarter of a century.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some people say that we should wait and consider the results of all the studies made, before undertaking some ourselves. I think that it is normal and appropriate for this parliament to start a personal investigation on all possible economic implications of a provincial secession, whether on the part of Quebec or another province, because we know that there are some other provinces which really need all their economic means, and are ready to go as far as separation to obtain or regain them.
Yet, I hope that this investigation will not be made in the spirit suggested by the hon. Minister of Finance, when, yesterday, he declared himself certain-as if he had given some instructions on the manner in which this investigation was to be made when it gets under way-that no investigation into the Canadian situation could end in favour of Quebec separatism.
And he added, as reported in Le Devoir:
It could In no way favour a secession.
-when speaking of the inquiry.
Obviously, this remains to be proved. There is every reason to believe that the results of the inquiry might point that way, but I think

Federal-Provincial Relations it would be most unwise to anticipate the results of that investigation.
Various reliable persons throughout the country advanced very valid arguments, saying that there certainly were some economic advantages for the province of Quebec in being part of the confederation. Would there be adequate compensations? Quite possibly. The investigation will prove it. We should not anticipate the results.
I would like to say one last word. There was some mention of Canadian unity, and I am all for it. But if unity means loss of its personality for any one province, whether it be Quebec or another, but most particularly Quebec, and that unity also signifies the loss of the French Canadian character, we would not approve it. We agree that there should be a close and active co-operation between the two racial groups in Canada and between the various provinces.
If, however, unity means the loss of those personalities, we shall no longer agree. I am convinced beforehand the survey will show that Quebec would not remain within confederation if those considerations were disregarded.
I feel, however, that parliamentarians take a sufficiently general view of our national problems to understand this situation and to agree with the Prime Minister when he states that Quebec is not a province like the others and that it should not be treated like the other provinces.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STUDY OF EFFECT ON CANADA OF SEPARATION OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the opinion expressed by the Prime Minister a while ago, when he said that if the government refused to consider the problems which arise from time to time, it would be proof of inefficiency and an indication that it does not have the required courage to face its obligations.
I feel that a thorough study of the problems which arise in the economic, social and cultural fields should be made from time to time, periodically, to see exactly what is going on and what has taken place in all the provinces of Canada, and that such a study has been imperative for a long time; but between that and saying, for instance, that the purpose of such a study is to prove that our economy cannot be divided there is quite a difference, because while government experts endeavour in all Canadian provinces to settle or study economic, social and cultural problems, in some other provinces, namely in the province of Quebec, experts and economists are now making studies to see how far Quebec could be self-sufficient.
What is the use of making a secret of it? Everybody knows that such work has been going on in Quebec for many months; but this does not mean that Quebec will separate. This merely means-and this is a warning to the federal government-that it is time to have a sound national policy, to face facts and realize that the provinces must have more freedom, otherwise the time will come when we will live in a period of economic chaos which will please nobody in the country and no province.
Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec can be different from the others, but all it asks of the federal government-just as the other provinces do at the federal-provincial conferences-is what it is entitled to and nothing else. It is not requested that another province be emptied to fill the province of Quebec. Such is not the case, but the province of Quebec should be allowed, like the others, to develop in a natural way, to accomplish its emancipation according to its aspirations, its life, its culture and its physical possibilities.
That is why the Ralliement Creditiste informed the federal government, several months ago, that we claim for Quebec: 1. The control of credit, which will solve the monetary question in our province, and also in the other provinces.
2. Decentralization to the point of letting the provinces deal with their immigration problem. That is that what we are asking for the province of Quebec.
I just heard an hon. member say that makes him laugh. Mark my words, he will not be laughing so much in his riding at the next election.
Mr. Speaker, the third point is the control of our imports and exports and the return of taxation rights to the provinces.
The government should seriously consider those points and, at federal-provincial conferences, act upon the economic, social and cultural study the experts are now making and which, I hope, will result in a better understanding between the provinces that will enable us to celebrate not, as will be the case tomorrow July 1, a confederation that is going down the river, but a revitalized, living renovated confederation, a confederation in which each province would be allowed to develop according to its aspirations and possibilities.

I should like to make a brief statement concerning the St. Lawrence seaway tolls review.
The governments of Canada and the United States have exchanged notes approving a supplemental agreement to the 1959 agreement between the St. Lawrence seaway authority and the Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation with respect to the St. Lawrence seaway tariff of tolls. The supplemental agreement provides that:
(a)	The date for the entities to report to their respective governments as to the sufficiency of seaway tolls will be deferred from July 1, 1964 to July 1, 1966, and the developmental period of the seaway will thereby be extended by two years and will be deemed to terminate at the end of the 1966 navigation season. Accordingly, no change in tolls will be proposed at the present time.
(b)	The joint review will be continued and at the conclusion of this two year extension tolls proposals will be related as realistically as possible to the financial requirements of the seaway entities.

I thank the hon. members for asking me to explain.
We all agree that there are many archaisms, not only in parliamentary procedure but also in the constitution. I feel that the best means to ward off what everyone dreads, separatism, is to strengthen our Canadian purpose which, unfortunately is not prevalent enough in Canada.
To strengthen this purpose, this ideal, our constitution must be modernized. The purpose of this bill is to remove from the text of the constitution theoretical rights which have not been exercised for many decades such as the federal parliament right of disallowance on provincial statutes.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. P. Deschaielets (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: ERECTION OF SCAFFOLDING OUTSIDE PEACE TOWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) asked me a question yesterday concerning the exterior work being done at present on the peace tower.
I should like to say that the scaffolding which, in his opinion, mars the appearance of parliament will be removed this afternoon and the contractor will no longer have to use it.
The work will be completed in approximately six weeks. I have asked the contractor to expedite matters and to employ additional men if possible to work overtime.

The house resumed, from Wednesday, June 17, consideration of the motion by Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.

Canadian Flag
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we celebrate another national birthday, our 97th, without a flag. "Canada does not have an official national flag-"
Yes.

Mr. Speaker, I hear interjections from the official opposition. Those are not my words, so perhaps I should read them very carefully:
Canada does not have an official national flag, but flies several which are regulated by custom, parliamentary act and orders In council. The union flag or jack, as it is commonly called, and the Canadian red ensign are the two most frequently flown by private persons and by public as well as governmental bodies. The Canadian red ensign is frequently flown both at home and abroad when a distinctly Canadian flag is considered desirable. Much heat is engendered by discussions over what flag should be adopted: indeed, their design has become something of a recurrent national pastime. So far successive federal governments have considered it prudent to refrain from taking a definite line one way or another.
These are a few of the words carefully chosen by Dr. Conrad M. J. F. Swan, Rouge Dragon, College of Arms, London, the first Canadian to be appointed by a sovereign to the college. They are taken from his published paper entitled "The Canadian Arms of Dominion and Sovereignty" which was presented at the fifth international congress of geneological and heraldic science held in Stockholm, Sweden, in 1960. This study is painstaking in its review of relevant authorities. Dr. Swan was speaking to a world body of experts.
Of all commonwealth countries, Canada has been the most careless respecting her colours. Without any underlying reason we stumbled into the use of the sea flag to designate our nation, the sea flag of the British merchant marine recognized as such all over the world. This is a presumption that should not be permitted to continue, a practice that has added little to Canada's dignity in foreign eyes.
The Recorder and Times of Brockville published on its editorial page recently this remark by a British visitor:
Why are some of your people determined to hang onto a flag which never really belonged to you?
The sad fact, Mr. Speaker, is that Canada has remained too ignorant or too stubborn to conform to established British flag usage as a colony while at the same time she has 
been unwilling to assume the badge of a nation. This state of affairs is unworthy of a country about to enter its second century.
Let us hope that out of this flag chaos, for chaos it is, there may come order and beauty. It is time we had a flag to represent our own, our native land; and what is better than this long established sprig of sugar maple to portray us to ourselves and to the world? If this resolution carries we will have a banner that sends the clean and clear message "Canada" in such winsome form as to merit, I believe, the gratitude of our children and the rectorship of judgment.
Sir Charles G. D. Roberts loved Britain but pledged his allegiance to his own country. In his poem "Canada" he wrote:
How long the ignoble sloth, how long
The trust in greatness not thine own?
Surely the lion's brood is strong
To front the world alone!
How long the indolence, ere thou dare
Achieve thy destiny, seize thy fame,
Ere our proud eyes behold thee bear
A nation's franchise, nation's name?
The purpose of a new flag is to bear our name, the name Canada, and a Canada extending from sea to sea. And what about this flag about to be born, about to flutter on our plains and on our mountains, as well as on the far places of the earth? "I am not the flag; not at all. I am but its shadow. I am whatever you make me, nothing more. I am your belief in yourself, your dream of what a people may become. I am the day's work of the weakest man, and the largest dream of the most daring. I am no more than you believe me to be and I am all that you believe I can be. I am whatever you make me, nothing more."
This new flag will be what our brave brothers of the Royal 22nd and the Royal Canadian Dragoons make it to be in Cyprus, the banner of the peacemaker in a dangerous and frightened world. This is a flag of which our young men shall see visions and our old men shall dream dreams. It is our reminder that notwithstanding the love we hold for the lands of our origins our allegiance must be to the land of our children. We are today witnessing a Canada come of age. Permit me, Mr. Speaker, to close in the words of Milton:'
Methinks I see in my mind a noble and puissant nation rousing herself like a strong man after sleep, and shaking her invincible locks.

And what happened?

Canadian Flag
I will read the words of Mr. Abbott, who was then a member of the government.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: He was just a private member then.

I am corrected; he was just a member sitting on a government side. He said:
It seems to me no useful purpose Is going to be served by an interminable debate in this house or outside it as to the desirability or otherwise of this plebiscite. We are going to have it, and in spite of what some people may say it is a thoroughly democratic procedure. I spoke a moment ago about responsibility and I suggest that the people of the country as a whole now have an opportunity to assume their responsibility, to turn out and vote and show each other and the rest of the world, if you will, that democracy can be made to work even in wartime.
I use those words and repeat them today to illustrate the point that to give the people a chance to express themselves on that issue was a demonstration to Canadians and to the world that even in time of war Canada could face up to an issue in a democratic way. The people certainly did. The majority voted yes. The minority, with deep feelings, voted no. They had their chance to express their feelings in a universal ballot. When conscription was brought about there was aquiescence and in most cases loyal support for the decision. What could have been a terribly divisive force capable of dividing Canada for generations was subdued because the government even in wartime took time out to let the people speak.
Hon. members might let their minds go back to the deep feelings which were expressed against conscription in 1942, not only in Quebec but all across this country. Had that parliament, with all the constitutional authority it possessed, imposed conscription on the people of Canada without holding a plebiscite, then today, more than 20 years later, this country would still be divided on that issue.
You cannot expect a large group of people in a democratic state to be forced into an action they do not like. But give that minority a chance to express itself in a democratic way and the result might well be different. When it was clear in 1942 to all those in every part of Canada who opposed conscription that the majority did not share their view, even those who had opposed it acquiesced. And, to their honour, when conscription was ultimately introduced many of them loyally sup-
ported the government and served this country at home and abroad in the uniform of His Majesty.
I have called attention to this precedent because we are faced now with another emotional issue. This time it is a different group which feels itself to be a minority. I should like to suggest to all those who want to ram this proposed flag down our throats immediately that they should consider the feelings of those groups in Canada which want to remember this country as being founded by French and English alike in a common purpose and sharing a common destiny. They want their symbols to show that common background. Their feelings on this subject of a flag are equally deep.
This is not a subject for great wisdom; it is not a subject for great lawyers and constitutional experts; it is not a subject for flag experts and those who deal with these things. It is a matter upon which the views of every individual, no matter how small he may be physically and mentally, are just as important as those of all the experts gathered together. This is an emotional issue. Large groups in Canada feel their deepest feelings have been assaulted; that the feelings which they and their fathers grew up with have been steamrollered, and I could use other expressions which only those close to the earth would understand. These are their feelings. They may be wrong, but I suggest they feel just as deeply as the people felt in 1942 on conscription. They want to express their opinions.
Read the words of the members who were opposed to conscription in that debate. Many of them supported a plebiscite. Some said "Yes, if the majority approves it, we will abide by it." Today I plead with the house and particularly with those on the government benches. Because you have 128 members over there and we have 95 or 96 over here, you do not have to trample us into the dust on this question. I would like to see it recognized in 1964 that there is a minority in Canada which feels deeply on this matter of the flag, and I suggest that if this flag is pushed through now without their say-so, this minority will grow and grow; it cannot help but grow. If this flag is forced on those who do not want it there will be an irreconcilable minority for decades to come, just as there would have been with regard to conscription in 1942 if parliament had forced through the house a measure to impose conscription on people across Canada who felt as deeply as they did against it,

without giving them an opportunity to express their views. However, when they were given an opportunity to do so and when they saw, after a long period of discussion, that the majority did want conscription, to their honour they not only acquiesced but, in their thousands, loyally supported that decision.
It is the same situation today, only in reverse. The groups I have mentioned are loyal Canadians. They have called for a referendum so their views may be measured. They have said that if the referendum or plebiscite goes against them they will be loyal to the flag which the majority of Canadians choose. What more could you ask from them? The situation was just as it is today, when everyone of us is loyal to those flags which fly on parliament hill today because legally it is the only distinctive flag we have.
Hear, hear.

Many thousands of men- not all of them-who fought in the last war believed they were proving to the world that it was their flag; and now we are told it is not. I simply suggest that the majority of the Canadian Legion have surely earned, by their sweat, their loneliness and their service, the right to have their views considered on this matter.
Hear, hear.

When they were stuck in those platoons on the fighting fronts of the world in 1942, 1943 and 1944 and waited for reinforcements, they saw their government delay and have a discussion over a plebiscite and a vote and then take a long time to put in conscription. Some of us are old enough to remember the bitter words that were said on those battlefields. But looking back at that situation today in retrospect we realize that if that plebiscite had not been given in 1942 there would have been a country divided against itself even today. Perhaps many a Canadian boy is not back here today because the government was slow; but looked at in retrospect, that move eased the pressure and subdued the deep feelings that were there, because they had a democratic chance to speak their piece by marking in the word "yes" or "no".
That is what this amendment asks for today. Surely considering the political realities, as they were considered in wartime, if you can take time out to bring in conscription in the middle of a war, and when there are deep feelings on this issue today-and these feelings will increase on a matter such as this-
Canadian Flag
and we want to maintain unity, we should give consideration to holding a plebiscite on this question of the flag. I suggest that when you already have the promise of these organizations that if the vote goes against them they will accept the new flag and loyally serve under it wherever duty calls, with that pledge you should honour the wish of the Canadian Legion at this time.
I am not going to delve into the intricate problems of the wording of the plebiscite. In my own mind I have gone through this many times. I want to keep the force of the suggestion I am making, which I think is a common sense type of logic, so clear that the people can make up their minds whether a plebiscite should or should not be used on this occasion. I think if the people looked at this situation with all the political realities as they are-and the whole country both east and west wants this country more united- here is one way that I suggest would help. Whether there is going to be, if this plebiscite idea is accepted, a committee of intellectuals, a committee of this house, or even a committee representing the provincial governments, regardless of what type of group you get together to plan the bare terms of this plebiscite I think a plebiscite could be worked out whereby the great majority of these people who now feel they are a minority would feel they had a chance to express themselves.
My final point to the house is this. If this democratic procedure, in the face of the political realities in Canada today, is not followed, then this flag debate may well become the turning point in Canada's history. The issue, as I see it, is whether to reinforce division or reinforce unity. When you have the pledge of these loyal organizations that they will support a referendum or plebiscite and will honour any decision that is taken by the majority, surely that is the way of unity. If you force a flag on the country without a vote you will leave a non-reconciled group on an issue on which it is vital to Canada that there be maximum unity.
I would appeal to those who have felt for many years in Canada that they are a continuing minority. I refer to those who come from the province of Quebec. Surely if you wish us who do not live in the province of Quebec to be always considerate of your position as a minority on issues that affect you deeply, such as your language, your culture and your religion-and believe me, in this country long before confederation and

Canadian Flag
since many of us have honoured those commitments-now that we have those with other loyalties in the maritimes, in the eastern townships, along the Ottawa river on the Quebec side, through many parts of Ontario-
What about the prairies?

-yes, and through the parts settled by new Canadians on the prairies, and in that old province of British Columbia, you will give this opportunity to those who feel deeply about and adhere to the flag. Give this to those who look not on the union jack as their flag at the moment but on the red ensign; who are proud of the fact that it has religious significance to them, with the crosses of St. George, St. Andrew and St. Patrick on it; who are conscious of the fact that many of them left their lands in Europe to get the protection of the principles of law and justice which that flag has spread all over the world. Whether you live in Burma, India, Pakistan, New Zealand or Australia the principles of law and justice under that flag carry on regardless of what new type of government they have. These people should have the right to ask from the government a chance to use their democratic right to express their opinion; and this is all they do ask.
I have heard people say "They had a chance in the last election. They will get a chance in the next election". This argument does not hold, because such a great body of our country, when you are voting Liberal against Conservative, against N.D.P., against Social Credit and against Creditiste, consider that other issues are far more important and they will not vote precisely on the flag issue. This is why many people who are Liberal today do not want a change in the flag. If an election was fought on the issue-and many other issues would have to go along with that- they would vote for the Liberal party because they are more Liberal than they are interested in the flag. The result is that you will leave on the flag issue this unsatisfied minority which will be there for 10, 15 or 20 years- for as long as they live.
Now, you could use another choice. You could slap in this flag and then by propaganda try to convince the people of this country, even though it has no background-I think someone once said that if you cross a horse and a mule you get a jackass-no posterity and certainly no promise for the future.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Don't bray so loud over there.

I should like to think that if you were going to win support for this new

flag you should face the political realities. Those who support the red ensign today know that much of their battle was lost because they were betrayed by the ministers of education in the provincial governments. Hardly a province in Canada today which has complete constitutional power over its schools has regulation to the effect that the legal flag of this country, the red ensign, must be flown. We have hundreds of thousands of school children who think that the union jack is Canada's flag. It is not; it is the flag of a sister member of the commonwealth. It is a proud flag but it is not ours. Hundreds of thousands of school children have no knowledge of our flag because they never see the flag of their country when they walk to school in the morning and come out of it at night. If the government does bring in a new flag, what good is it to us? After a while the C.B.C. loses interest. After a while the news media lose interest. It is a five day or maybe a nine day wonder. Until our school children see that flag every day and are told what men have endured for that flag, it is a meaningless thing.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the government cannot sell this new flag until they have the support of the provincial governments. And what do we find in this regard? British Columbia is going to fly four flags, and the other provinces will reveal their intentions in due course. I am simply suggesting that when the government have learned so much from the mistakes they made last year in trying to do everything in 60 days, with 300 days to regret it, why do they not adopt on such an emotional issue what I think is a reasonably logical and common sense approach, and if they are thinking of the long range unity of this country and of all people being behind this new flag in the course of a few years they could give to the present minority the same rights as another minority got in 1942. It is not on many issues that referendums and plebiscites should be used to take over the responsibility of the House of Commons; but I certainly believe that history has supported the plebiscite of 1942 and I should hope that history would support a plebiscite on the flag issue in 1965.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment moved by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) that a plebiscite be held on this very important issue. Before proceeding I must in fairness say that in doing so I am expressing my personal opinion;

but in expressing that opinion 1 am expressing the opinion of many of my constituents and, I am quite confident, of a large segment of the Canadian people. However, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am very glad to belong to a party that protects the rights of the minorities which exist within it.
To indicate the views of many of my constituents on this question I wish to table a petition which was circulated by the young Progressive Conservatives association of Rossland and Trail in Kootenay West, which contains the signatures of something over 900 citizens of our district and which represents the views of members or supporters of all parties which exist in that constituency, the four major parties. As you know, Mr. Speaker, we have not the fifth party in Kootenay West. The petition reads as follows:
We, the undersigned, believe Canada's heritage and future can be best symbolized only by the red ensign, bearing witness to her origins and the fundamental cultures from which will stem her future greatness. No twig of leaves alone can achieve this.
I wish to hand to the page boys this petition, which is 70 feet long and is signed by the good burghers of Kootenay West.

Mr. Speaker, I object to the printing of this petition in Hansard. We heard that the petition included 18,000 names. You can imagine what would happen if it were printed in Hansard. We would have a 3 foot thick volume. Consequently, as far as I am concerned, I object to the publication of this petition in Hansard.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member misunderstands my intentions. I am not asking for the names to be printed, I am asking for the petition to be tabled.
In that case, Mr. Speaker, I have no objection.

Then I am very glad we are in agreement on that question anyway, Mr. Speaker.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if you and the hon. members of the house will pardon a personal reference, I feel that my Norman, my English and my North American Indian ancestry provide me with a background that prompts me to respect all points of view and be able to deal with this question objectively, fairly and without undue emotion.
Canadian Flag
It is quite obvious that the flood of mail which members of the house are receiving on the flag issue indicates that many people's feelings are aroused to a far greater extent than they have been on some economic or social issues. That appears illogical on the surface but it is the fact. Something over 1,000 of my constituents have indicated to me their preference for the red ensign, and I think some six or eight have indicated their support for the proposed flag of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). I contrast that with receiving on a very important issue 10 postcards. It just means simply that people are human and that many take for granted that the other issues will be dealt with by parliament and proceeded with according to their wishes. But people do get concerned over an issue such as this, which indicates that support for symbols can stir people to action who otherwise are not in the habit of writing to members of parliament or expressing themselves in vigorous language. While on the surface this may appear to be illogical, in my opinion it is a healthy sign which demonstrates that multitudes of Canadians still consider ideals before dollars or material values. There is a good aspect to this, and I do not think we should underestimate it.
Now, fortunately, we live in a democracy where people can freely express their opinions and make a choice. Some people prefer abstract art to some of the great masters, others prefer Ezra Pound to the reading of Shakespeare; others prefer Elvis Presley to Beethoven. It is their right in a democracy to choose. In the same spirit of freedom; therefore, some will choose the Prime Minister's flag in preference to the red ensign.
Another interesting thing, Mr. Speaker, is that all parties are divided. We recognize that. It is obvious from the frequent remarks and interjections made by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) and some of his confreres from Quebec that the Progressive Conservative party is divided. There is nothing wrong with that on an issue of this type. The Liberal party is also divided on this issue. I have a very good indication of that. I see the hon. lady member for a Winnipeg constituency looking with some concern, but I shall have to inform her to that effect. Mr. H. M. Copp, of Vancouver, past president of the Vancouver-Burrard Liberal association, wrote a letter in which he said:
Many Liberals, including myself, will never fly the proposed new flag unless the decision to replace the red ensign is made by all Canadians

Canadian Flag
Suppose the Postmaster General issued a stamp showing the Postmaster General shooting down a stork in full flight. We would wonder whether he was going to adopt the bill that has been proposed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie). It would keep us all on the alert. There are endless possibilities to the announcement of government policy by the issuing of stamps. We think that policy should be announced in the house and that members of the house and the people of Canada should not be kept in a highly nervous state from day to day trying to read the meaning of government policy from the stamps that are issued from time to time. We think that was a blunder.
Fifth, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion it was a blunder for the Prime Minister to address the opening ceremonies of the annual convention of the Royal Canadian Legion at Winnipeg on this issue. While some have lauded him for his courage, and you can look at it from both points of view, it appears to me that in view of the announced policy of the Legion and the very strongly held and expressed views on the part of the great majority of the membership of the Legion, his speaking on this issue at their annual convention was a venture similar in nature to the leader of the New Democratic party addressing a nominating convention of the Progressive Conservative party on the virtues of socialism.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: A good idea.

I think that was a big mistake. It caused unnecessary misunderstanding and unnecessary heat to be generated over this important question. At this point I want to take the strongest exception to a cartoon that was published in the Citizen some two or three weeks ago with respect to the Royal Canadian Legion and which I thought portrayed veterans in a very undignified way. I think it was entirely uncalled for. None of us minds seeing a bit of wit and humour in a cartoon, and some sharp thrusts, but I think it is going a bit too far to depict aging veterans of this country sitting around a table drinking beer and content to remain as bloated windbags. I think this was a most unfortunate cartoon. It has been strongly resented by members of the Legion and their dependants and by many other Canadians. In my opinion it was in very poor taste indeed.
It is wonderful how news travels, Mr. Speaker, and I am wondering whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) has tipped off some of his friends in

the United States with regard to what he expects is going to happen. The new flag proposed by the Prime Minister is being flown over buildings in New York and Washington, not public buildings but over department stores and other buildings owned by corporations and companies.
Already?

Yes. We have pictures of them. They have been told: It's all right, boys; go ahead. This is the free enterprise system. A sales pitch is already being made in the United States for the sale of the new Canadian flag. This is not being done because of any love for Canada. I am quite confident that behind this action are the usual mercenary instincts which prompt such persons to take advantage of any developing social situation, whether it be by increasing the price of land because of the building of new houses, or something else. They take advantage of the opportunity for their own profit. In any event, we know that the news has reached the United States.
I want to repeat that this is an important question. I respect any person's sincere view upon it, whatever his view is, but I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) that the issue is so important it can only be resolved to the satisfaction of the present and future generations by a plebiscite in which the Canadian people will have the opportunity to choose between the Prime Minister's proposed flag, the red ensign or some modification of the same, or some other flag.
I think this is necessary, and that the majority will accept the decision with good will. The Royal Canadian Legion has expressed its opinions strongly in that respect. So have a number of other well known organizations, and I have received a good many letters to that effect.
We should not get too alarmed because people become, as I said before, very concerned about this issue and a little bit worked up. I glory in the fact that Canadians are not altogether concerned with dollar issues. They are concerned with all of these issues related to ideals, related to history, and related to symbols which mean a great deal to all of us in western civilization, whatever those symbols may be.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that in view of the nature of the issue, the emotional nature of the issue and the close involvement of the people on this

account, and in view of the succession of blunders made by the Prime Minister in the handling of this issue, and in order to obtain a decision satisfactory to the majority of Canadians, it is necessary to support the amendment for the holding of a plebiscite throughout the country so that once and for all we can determine the wishes of the people with respect to a national flag.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I should like to make a comment about the petition which the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has presented to the house. I should like to refer the hon. member to standing order No. 70, on page 49 of the "Standing Orders of the House of Commons". Subsection 1 says this:
A petition to the house may be presented by a member at any time during the sitting of the house by filing the same with the Clerk of the house.
My understanding is that the interpretation of that particular standing order is that it is to be filed with the Clerk of the house in the Clerk's office. I should also refer to section 2 of the same standing order which says:
Any member desiring to present a petition in his place in the house must do so during routine proceedings and before introduction of bills.
I am sure the hon. member will recognize the meaning of that particular section and of the action which he has taken in tabling the petition after that period during the day. I might suggest to the hon. member that the better procedure would be for him to present the petition to the Clerk of the house in the Clerk's office.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you for your explanation. As one who always tries to keep the rules I trust I will not be named for this violation of the rules, and at the first opportunity I shall take the petition and present it to the Clerk in his office.

Mr. Speaker, we are all stiff from straining our history muscles in preparation for this debate. It is rather like term essay time in college. Seldom have the librarians been hurled into the battle so early and in such force. I know they welcome the pause which the delays in the debate have given them to clear away the debris of flag books, photocopies, old orders in council and crumpled library slips. They have been struck by a hurricane of heraldry.
Our flag history in the west is somewhat different from that of the rest of Canada, because we are different. The Hudson's Bay
Canadian Flag
Company was trading on the prairies before the American revolution, and long before United Empire Loyalists were heard of. They had their charter from Charles II in 1570, just three years after the birth of Champlain, the 400th anniversary of whose birth incidentally is celebrated in our centennial year. They also had permission to fly the red ensign with the letters H.B.C. in the fly as their company flag. This flag flew over trading posts and forts when John A. Macdonald was a child. It flies over our Hudson's Bay stores in the west today and will continue to fly over them after Canada has adopted the maple leaf flag. Thus, the government of Canada was not the first to fly the red ensign in British North America.
The Canadian red ensign is not a unique and distinctive flag within Canada. We have another and an older one in the west. I wish to extend to all members of this house who may feel an unbearable nostalgia for the red ensign, and particularly to my good friend the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), who, unfortunately, is not here this afternoon, an invitation to visit the beautiful city of Vancouver and shop under the old H.B.C. red ensign, six days a week and to nine o'clock on Friday evenings.
Nor is the red ensign distinctive outside Canada. In a window in Toronto airport you may see today a display of world flags among which are seven British ensigns, blue and red, including our own. If you carried the red ensign across Texas, do you really believe that anyone would say, "Hello, Canada"?
They sure would.

Like a woman wondering what to wear, Canada has never been able to make her mind up about a flag. John Bouri-not, a clerk of the House of Commons, who sat in the very same chair which Mr. Raymond occupies with such distinction today, wrote a book in 1895 called: "How Canada is Governed". In it he said this about our flags:
The union jack is flown from all fortresses and garrisons of Canada. The Dominion of Canada has also authority to display on all public occasions a national flag, viz., the red or blue ensign. The red ensign is displayed at the opening and closing of parliament, and on national occasions.
The custom of flying the red ensign in Canada appears to have originated before confederation. Sir Edmund Head, later to be governor of the Canadas, wrote to Lord Grey in 1851 saying: "Their flag should be a modification of our own with a difference of some kind." Thus, the idea of an ensign or modified

Canadian Flag
union jack stems, not from Canadian minds, but from the colonial office.
Sir John A. Macdonald apparently encouraged this idea by flying the red ensign on parliament hill. As a Scot, he was probably no union jack lover. James VI had made the first union jack when he slapped England's cross of St. George on top of the cross of St. Andrew and told the fiercely protesting Scots to like it or lump it. Scottish loyalty to the flag today expresses more their increasing equity and proprietorship in England than their brotherly love of Englishmen.
An illustration in Canadian Illustrated News of February 26, 1870, shows the red ensign on the parliament buildings without any identifying crest or badge on the fly. I think I am historically correct in saying that the first red ensign flown on the House of Commons was the undefaced marine ensign, flown by Sir John A. Macdonald in the very first years of confederation. It appears to have flown there regularly until 1904 when a curious incident occurred. On St. Patrick's day, Mr. Henri Bourassa, the member for Labelle and the Rene Levesque of his day, rose in the house and said:
"I noticed on the day of the opening of parliament as well as today, which is St. Patrick's day, that the Canadian flag which used to be put up on the tower of parliament buildings has been replaced by a union jack. I would like to know why the old flag that has been used in Canada ever since confederation should be laid aside".
I can think of no one less likely to champion the flag of Sir John A. Macdonald than Henri Bourassa, unless it were Louis Riel himself. Yet there he was calling upon Sir Wilfrid Laurier to explain what he had done with Sir John's flag.
Sir Wilfrid rose, and if he is remembered for his courtly manners and gracious speech he wasn't wasting any of them on his rival that day. He said:
I am sorry to say that I cannot satisfy today the rather fastidious curiosity of my hon. friend but I will make inquiry and try to give him an explanation upon another day.
Mr. Bourassa replied: "Perhaps the British empire league has something to do with it".
Then the Hon. James Sutherland, minister of public works, spilled the beans. He said:
I may explain to the hon. gentleman that the flag hitherto flown on the parliament buildings has been what is known as the Canadian merchant marine flag. It is not the national flag in any other sense. The national flag, as we understand it for this purpose, is the union jack. Many complaints have reached the department on previous occasions that the flag floating over the parliament buildings was not the authorized flag for that

purpose, and when we were buying a new flag the one which was bought, in accordance with the custom of Canada and all portions of the empire throughout the world, was the one authorized for the purpose.
Quite a different story than the one given by Bourinot in 1895. Then Mr. Bourassa said:
I know that the red ensign is the merchant marine flag but I know it has always been used in this country as being the special colonial flag to which we have added the escutcheon of confederation. It has always been used on the building.
There the matter was dropped. Not a tear from a Tory as Sir Wilfrid pulled down the red ensign and stuffed it into the flag locker- only the plaintive protest of Henri Bourassa. Sir John A. Macdonald had introduced the red ensign to Canada simply by running it up the pole like the jolly roger, when he swarmed aboard the ship of state; and Laurier had struck it from the mast the same way.
Years later in May, 1931, Mr. Cameron McIntosh, then the member for North Battle-ford referred to the incident. He said:
Before 1904 we had the red ensign with the coat of arms of Canada in the fly, which flag was our flag from the days of Sir John A. Macdonald down to 1904. The flag was flown across this country from ocean to ocean; it was the national flag from Atlantic to Pacific. However, it was hauled down in 1904. Why? The circumstances surrounding the taking down of that flag have never been made known to the Canadian people but it was taken down and from 1904 to the present day the union jack has been flown in its place. In 1912 the union jack was made the official flag of Canada by the secretary of state for the colonies and from 1912 to 1931 as from 1904 to 1912 the union jack has been flown in Canada as our Canadian flag-something distinctly it can never be. The red ensign, differenced by the Canadian coat of arms, is flying outside of Canada, but it is not the official flag in Canada, it was hauled down and has never been put up.
The Conservatives were in power in 1931. They could have restored Sir John's red ensign to its place on top of the peace tower. The tower was there, but they chose not to. They left it for Mackenzie King to do that in 1945.
King, at heart a red ensign man, was always under suspicion of performing some jiggery-pokery with the flag. As long ago as May 31, 1929, Mr. Thomas Donnelly asked this hair-raising question:
I would like to ask the Prime Minister if a committee has been appointed, as stated, consisting of six or seven Roman Catholic priests to provide a new flag for Canada.
While I am debunking some history, I want to return to the prairies at the time of confederation. I have said that the flag which flew in the early west was the red ensign of the Hudson's Bay Company.

When Riel took Fort Garry in 1869 the Metis pulled down the company flag and ran up the flag of the provisional government, which bore the fleur-de-lis for their French origin, and shamrocks in honour of William O'Donaghue, Fenian and friend of Riel.
In the spring of 1870, Riel pulled this flag down and ran up the union jack as an indication of his provisional government's willingness to co-operate with Ottawa. When O'Donaghue tried to pull down the union jack, Riel called Andre Nault, the man who commanded the firing squad which shot Scott, and ordered him to shoot anyone who tried to pull down the union jack. The whole story is told in Davidson's life of Louis Riel.
Thus, Riel became a sort of Canadian Barbara Frietchie:
Shoot if you must this old gray head,
But spare your country's flag, she said.
Western flags do not end with the Metis flag, and the Hudson's Bay Company flag. We have a British Columbia flag which we acquired quite as casually as Canada acquired the red ensign from Sir John A. Macdonald. One day, about two years ago, Mr. Bennett came home from a visit to England and announced that he had found the flag of British Columbia in the catacombs of the college of heralds, where it had lain unseen by man for many years, like the body of Tutankhamen.
It consisted of a union jack, a series of wavy blue bands to represent the Pacific ocean and shooting up over the whole thing the rays of a big yellow setting sun. Harold Weir, a Vancouver Sun columnist, put on sun glasses against any possible injury and went out to see it. He described it as a "startling salmagundy of form and colour". I looked up "salmagundy" and found it was a meat salad of many ingredients. I see many B.C. flags around these days, and I will say this for them; they are certainly bright and cheerful.
Today this flag, along with the red ensign and union jack, are flown on poles all the same height-on the grounds of the legislature in Victoria. In a statement to Canadian Press, Mr. Bennett said:
If parliament approves the proposed maple leaf flag it will be flown in front of the legislature but only in addition to the three flags being raised -the ensign, the union jack and the B.C. flag.
Although I am hesitant to break the news to him, for fear what it may do to his mind, I must tell the hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) that in British Columbia we will have not two flags -not three flags-but four flags.
Canadian Flag
We do not need another flag in the west. We have plenty of them now and we are loyal to them all in our own fashion. Visiting American Rotarians are already confused by the several flags blazing behind the head table. They do not know which way to turn when the anthem is played. How can we explain another one to them?
If Canada were the west alone, I do not believe we would choose a new flag now. Some would agitate for one. Most would be content to keep our old banners. If the choice were ours we would not choose a maple leaf. The sugar maple is not a part of the west. The buffalo, the wheat sheaf and-on the totems of our coastal Indians-the thunder-bird; these are the symbols of the west. Yes, even the old red ensign of the Hudson's Bay Company. How distant and how unreal the battle seems. We are 3,000 miles from the bicultural front. The aspirations of Quebec are interpreted to us by the Anglo-Saxons of Ontario, and sometimes I think they lose a little in translation. We hear the voice of Quebec on the second or third echo.
How easy it would be for western members in this debate to vote for a plebiscite. We could drop our parliamentary responsibilities with the easy abandon of Gypsy Rose Lee dropping her beads. We could leave it to the men in the wheat fields, the girls in the offices and the boys on the fish boats to vote for the flag-or to vote against it. Then, when barnyard patriots had won the day, we could come back and shout at our French Canadian brothers in the house: We have a mandate from our people and we are here to impose it on you.
Come, let us reason together. Is this what we in honesty believe we should do to Canada? Are we to go to the two million Europeans and Asians who live in the west and ask them for a mandate to shove a flag which flew at the masthead of Wolfe's ship down the throats of five and a half million of their fellow Canadians who live 3,000 miles away? Said Lord Durham, of the Canadas in 1839: "I found two nations warring ... the children lisped the hatred they would feel as men". Will it be any different if we fail in this debate to find the meaning of Canada?
In his address on the flag, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) singled out the ridings of Victoria and Vancouver. I have singled out the city of Prince Albert, perhaps a more typical western city, to illustrate my case. These are the people who live there: 11,331 British, 3,560 French,

Canadian Flag
226 Austrians, 67 Czechs and Slovaks, 16 Finns, 1,764 Germans, 280 Hungarians, 46 Italians, 94 Jews, 551 Dutch, 1,063 Poles, 210 Russians, 1,891 Scandinavians 2,260 Ukrainians, 174 Chinese, 225 native Indians, and 410 from other countries. There are 24,168 people in Prince Albert. The minority are of British origin. I would sooner toss a skunk into a Sunday school picnic rather than set the good people of Prince Albert against each other on the subject of a distinctive Canadian flag versus a flag of British design and origin.
What absolute nonsense.

Kennedy said:
With a good conscience our only sure reward, with history the final judge of our deeds, let us go forth to lead the land we love-
That is what we were asked to do when we were elected-to lead the land we love. We are sent here to participate in the political leadership of Canada. For my part, I willingly accept that responsibility for the people of Vancouver Quadra.
I believe a plebiscite would be a beast let loose on the land to tear at the guts of national unity.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is a very profound statement.

I believe Canada needs not only a distinctive flag but a distinctive Canadian spirit. Wolfe and Montcalm were not Canadians; they were two lonely imperial soldiers fighting a battle thousands of miles from home. They had no personal links with Canada, no interest in her destiny, no Canadian spirit. The forgotten man whom Canadians should remember was Abraham Martin, a 17th century Scot who died exactly 400 years ago. He married a French girl, came to Quebec, and eventually acquired the lands on which the battle was fought a century later, the plains of Abraham. No Canadian traces his name to Wolfe and Montcalm, but hundreds, perhaps thousands, do to the Scottish-French couple who were among the first Canadians. We built a statue to the victor and vanquished and forgot the Canadian couple, Martin, who triumphed by doing what comes naturally.
I ask those who wrote to me to say Quebec should shove off, to read Vincent Massey's speech in Charlottetown on Monday, June 1, 1964, in which he said:
If the maintenance of our east and west links is questioned as a national policy, the doubters are men who fail to understand the land in which they live...We have two founding races, French and

English in origin, their languages and cultures having a special and permanent place in the national scene. That is an historical fact, not a political judgment.
I ask all those who sent me pictures of the red ensign, patriotic poems and prayers, to remember the words of Arthur Meighen which he spoke on the occasion of the planting of maples in the cemetery at Vimy Ridge in 1921:
Above them are being planted the maples of Canada in the thought that her sons will rest the better in the shade of the trees they knew so well in life.
Do you believe, if they could speak, they would reject a maple leaf flag for Canada? Finally, I ask that under our new flag each of us, west and east, strives to make this nation such an example of unity at home and integrity abroad that people will recognize our flag, wherever in the world it is flown, and say with pleasure "Hello, Canada".
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker; it is obvious that the hon. member was reading from a document. I wonder if he would care to identify that document.
I will be very glad to identify it, Mr. Speaker. The document was copious notes which I had prepared-
Notes. You read every word of it.
Are you jealous?

-from various books
available in the library of parliament to every member of the house. I will be glad to identify to my hon. friend the sources of my information and make available my notes, if they are of value to him. I am sure he is really asking because he feels they would be of some value to him.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable interest and attention to what has been said by the hon. members who have participated in this debate. What I am about to say reflects the feelings of the Royal Canadian Legion, the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire and a great number of other Canadians who have felt keenly enough about this issue to take the time to write letters-

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. It has just been pointed out, on the Conservative side, that speeches should not be read in the house. Now, the hon. member who has just risen is beginning to read a text

he has before him. I would like to call his attention on the point of order which was raised by his colleague, a few moments ago.

Mr. Speaker, on the point of order I wish to say that perhaps the minister is not aware of this, but in this House of Commons, ever since confederation I presume-at least, ever since I have been here-there has been such a thing as courtesy-
Hear, hear.

-and it has been general for Speakers to ignore the fact that new members may be reading from copious notes in their early speeches in this house. I resent the advantage that the minister has taken of this situation to raise this sort of point of order.
Shame.

On that point of order, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to point out to my hon. friend that we always allowed hon. members to read their texts. Objections have always been raised by members of his party. That is why I remind him that they always lacked courtesy, but we never did on this side of the house.

If I may continue, Mr. Speaker; I do not think the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) objected to having a little fun poked at him, and if the minister in question was not so thin skinned he would not have raised this question as a point of order.
You should listen carefully and you would learn that you are still in error.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, the previous member was not interrupted when he was making his speech. It is true that he was asked afterwards whether or not he had read from a manuscript, but he was not interrupted; and I think this member ought not to be interrupted. May I say to the minister that probably if he were to read some of his speeches inside and outside the house, he would not get his foot in his mouth so often.

Hear, hear.
