speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The point of order that has just been raised by the minister is now developing into a discussion. This point of order has been raised on a number of occasions previously. It was raised while I was in the chair, and at that time I referred hon. members to citation 144 of Beauchesne. By virtue of what is said therein, I am sure there is no difficulty about the hon. member continuing to make reference to his notes.
The hon. member for Victoria (Ont.).

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The letters to which I have referred were expressing disappointment with the choice of a Canadian flag, and the hope that the outcome of this debate would be the retention of the red ensign as Canada's national flag. The Prime Minister and his government have made their position very clear. They have chosen what they call a truly distinctive Canadian flag. Now the Canadian Legion and the people across Canada are making their stand known to members of parliament in every party, and in the final analysis it will be the vote of the individual member and senator, whether he be Liberal, Conservative, N.D.P. or Social Credit, that will decide what has become a crucial issue.
The Legion's fervent desire for the retention of the red ensign as the national flag of this land is, I believe, shared by the majority of their fellow Canadians. Surely the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) realizes the bitter feeling and disunity which this proposed flag will create in all parts of the country, instead of the harmony and unity that all patriotic Canadians earnestly desire. But there are always those who are not content to let well enough alone. For the past few years scores of people have been working diligently to design what is in their opinion the perfect symbol of our national existence. Like all other hon. members I have received dozens of suggested designs. But Canada has a distinctive national flag which takes its status from an order in council dated September 5, 1945, its use authorized "wherever it is desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag." That is the law so long as the order in council remains in force, and it is a blunder to divide the people of Canada at this time when it is clear that the change will encounter bitter resentment from a large part of our population.
Approximately 100,000 Canadians died on the battle fields during world wars I and II and in Korea, and many thousands of war casualties lie in military and public hospitals

Canadian Flag
throughout Canada still suffering from these conflicts. All these Canadians proudly served under the Canadian red ensign during time of war, and still wish to serve in time of peace under the same flag. Resistance to the idea of a new flag is based on the feeling that much of the sentiment in favour of a new design is a desire to weaken all signs of connection with the British empire, and all its traditions of freedom and peace.
The red ensign means something to Canadians that can never be wiped out. It is a symbol, and a nation's flag is full of meaning. We are told that the red ensign has no meaning for those ethnic groups who have emigrated to this country and become Canadians. I cannot accept that argument. Canadians comprise almost every race in the world today. These people came here from other lands by choice, knowing that the union jack and the red ensign were part of our history. In fact they were probably influenced by that very fact, because they are symbols of liberty, freedom and equality. Every Canadian, whether he be of English or French origin or an immigrant from Europe, owes much to British institutions and to British justice.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from an article in the Lindsay Post for Friday, June 5, 1964. There is a picture of the Fenian raid medal which was issued back in 1870 and was presented to a gentleman in my home town of Lindsay. This article says:
"This undignified uproar regarding a Canadian flag is obnoxious, at least it is to me", said R. W. Pitts of 80 Cambridge street north. He added, "The ensign goes a long way back in Canadian history. I have in my possession a medal I am very proud of because it bears the name of my father, Sergeant R. E. Pitts, who was in the army in the days of the Fenian raid. It is dated 1870, and is made of silver with a fine likeness of Her Majesty Queen Victoria, who was known as 'Queen Victoria the good' ".
On the reverse side of the medal appears the red ensign. It is quite discernible although it is showing the minor ravage of old age. At the bottom appears the coat of arms and on the edge is the name of Sergeant R. E. Pitts, 56th B.N.
The historic emblem of the days of the Fenian raid is supported by a ribbon of red, white and blue.
Sergeant Pitts, who was of Irish extraction, was born in Cornwall and participated in the Fenian raid which reached its climax at Niagara Falls. Canadian soldiers were strewn along the long stretch of the St. Lawrence river.
B- W. Pitts, of Lindsay, Sergeant Pitt's son, is the proud possessor of his father's medal.
For the benefit of hon. members who have not seen this medal I should like to hold up this paper, which shows a picture of both sides of the medal. This medal goes back to

1866 in the days of the Fenian raid, which reached its climax at Niagara Falls with fighting along the banks of the St. Lawrence river; and the red ensign was flown in those days. The reason I mention this, Mr. Speaker, is because I want to show why we should still uphold the red ensign.
Our real attachment to British institutions and their symbols is not chiefly one of sentiment, but an admiration of British justice and fair play, for freedom to live our own lives and worship according to the dictates of our own conscience without hindrance from any man. This genuine patriotism we can ask and expect any Canadian, of whatever race or language, to share with us as a common inheritance. It has been said, and rightly so, that a country which does not honour its past has no future.
The advocates of a new national anthem seem to have accepted "O Canada" as such, and have had some success in inducing others to accept it. But "O Canada" is no more Canada's national anthem than the "Maple Leaf Forever" which is a good deal older and to my mind not noticeably inferior. Canada's national anthem is "God Save the Queen". It has by usage been accepted by all the subjects of the British crown to express their devotion, and is honoured by the majority of Canadians. "O Canada" is more of a lament than an anthem, but for the last few years it has been used by the people at public gatherings as Canada's national anthem. Not one person in 20 can recite the words, and I believe there is both a French and English version. Brass bands can do very nice things with it; but it is not an anthem, and until someone can come up with something more suitable, let us keep "God Save the Queen".
In my home county of Victoria, Mr. Speaker, there are 25 reeves and deputy reeves. Victoria county takes in a large portion of one of the finest agricultural areas of Canada. At their meeting on Monday last the county council passed a resolution calling for the red ensign to be flown above county buildings and wherever a flag should be flown in any part of the county of Victoria, which covers a large area. I was very pleased to hear this. In closing I want to say I am very much in favour of the red ensign, and I will do all I can in my power to see that this great flag is retained as the national flag of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in the Montreal Star of June 16,

I read a dispatch from Paris where a correspondent indicated that Europeans did not know whether they should laugh or cry at the spectacle of a country such as Canada now being stirred by a debate on a flag.
At first, those people were amazed to learn that Canada did not have a flag. In certain quarters, it was understood that the Prime Minister's action, in his proposal for the choice of an emblem, was finally leading to the total emancipation of our country.
I am sure that such a reaction, which was noted in foreign countries, is also that of the great majority of the Canadian people.
Let us not complicate the matter ourselves. The people, great simplificators that they are, have understood for a long time. They know from instinct that if we do not have as yet a distinctive national emblem, the fault is imputable to their representatives. They have long judged the sterility of empty quibbling. They have confounded all sophisms. They wish and long for unity, and they always suspect that some instigators of dissension are craftily attempting to compromise that unity.
The people refuse to admit that, after 40 years of debates, the matter has made no progress in the minds of their representatives and that, even today, at this late hour, consideration is given to the possibility of unloading on them the responsibility of the choice to be made.
Those people, Mr. Speaker, who have every reason to be sceptical, have been waiting a long time for a definite commitment on the part of one of the national parties with regard to a flag of their own. Our people had lost their faith, so that, even faced with a categorical Liberal promise, they were still in doubt.
Today, the commitment has been kept, and the government is accomplishing what it promised to do, by submitting the design of a distinctive flag to the approval of the house.
I do not doubt for a single moment that the majority of hon. members will accept this design. I shall even go farther and say that the people are no more in doubt, and that they anticipated this assent in many areas by adopting the suggested flag of their own accord, the theme of which had immediately been recognized as a symbol which had been their own for a long time. They look upon it as distinctive, and the people now feel freer, prouder, more united; their country has suddenly become a more concrete fact, so that the various problems it has to face somehow seem less difficult to solve.
Canadian Flag
Each supporter of the new flag finds a brother everywhere between those blue stripes evoking the encircling oceans. He also knows that a giant stride forward has been made towards fulfilment. A flag which is truly his own will give the displaced person of yesterday, who is still pushed around today, a concrete sense of belonging, of living in his own context. It identifies his historic destiny, determines his ideal, gives a meaning to his life, while restoring a past which had been lost in the fog of history deprived of purpose.
With that flag, Mr. Speaker, a Canadian knows what he is. The emblem will crystallize his aspirations, toward unity first of all and toward his distinctive and initial career afterwards. The flag will do that, because it will make a number of other things possible.
That is why we must be careful that scandal does not come from us, in this house. The scandal would be to let this debate slowly turn into a circus. I am confident that will not happen. We all want to give our country the fundamental emblems essential to any sovereign country.
The choice of a distinctive flag is an act of sovereignty and maturity. It must be a compromise acceptable to all men of good faith. The flag must not divide but unite.
For decades unity has been the main theme of our speeches. This is the minute of truth. There is no escape through evasion or secret agreements. We must take a clear stand, say yes or no, and we members of parliament, must assume the responsibility for the choice to be made.
As for me, I would not want to be too finicky. The argument which justified the cabinet's choice seems reasonable to me. The proposed flag is distinctive. It reflects our political and military tradition. It pleases the eye and fulfils the standards of heraldry. Therefore, I shall be proud to pass it on to my descendants.
I shall be proud of having had the privilege to play a part in taking my country out of the no man's land of an anonymous, impersonal and spiritless humanity. And I shall have found at the same time, in my heart and reason, grounds to believe again that Canada is a viable country that can achieve a distinctive and fully satisfying destiny on this American continent.

Mr. Speaker, I find myself in some difficulty in following such logical and eloquent addresses as those delivered by hon. members who

Canadian Flag
have preceded me. The speech delivered by the hon. member tor Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) was logical and any person, even with legal training, would be proud of it. It impressed us. I think the addresses of all members on all sides of this house have impressed those who have been here. I am going to take neither the legal angle nor the constitutional angle in this debate. I go along with those who have referred to this as an emotional issue and feelings are running high. There are two sides in this house, and I think there are two sides in the country.
There are those who would accept anything, a maple leaf, a rabbit or anything, just to get rid of that cursed union jack we have been carrying on our flag. There are others, Mr. Speaker, who are just as anxious to retain that union jack, whether in one quarter of our flag or one eighth of our flag, just as long as it is there. I believe that both groups are sincere; both groups have arguments and this is the only forum in which those arguments can be presented. My only regret is that the government is trying to hurry this measure through the house. I was not surprised when some of those Afro-Asian nations, without a history, without a culture, without any background, which found themselves free, rushed to create symbols by which they would be recognized by their neighbours. Theirs was a case of necessity. Many of them probably took less than the nine day period of gestation that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) took to create his flag out of the thousands and thousands of designs that had been submitted to the government since a committee considered the matter in 1944 and 1945.
Macdonald, Cartier and the other fathers of confederation created what they thought was a nation, and why Canada on its 97th birthday should be fighting over the symbol of nationhood is hard for many people to understand. It must be hard for our allies in NATO to understand why we are fighting over our national symbol. It no doubt will be hard for the member nations of the United Nations to understand, because since we entered the field of international politics we have given them the impression that we had a flag.
I am one of those who feel that we have had and still have a flag, and I intend to quote authorities to show that I am not the only one who feels that way. There are thousands, in fact millions, who feel as I do. I am not going to be so bold as to say that a majority of the Canadian people are behind the red ensign, but I have just as much right
[Mr. Mandziuk.l
to express my view as those who want a distinctive flag with three leaves or one leaf, or what have you. I have just as much right to express my view as they do. I am going to quote other authorities who think as I do.
Since I entered the House of Commons in 1957 I have expressed my support for the red ensign and have given reasons. Others, too, have reasons. My first quotation is taken from the Winnipeg Tribune, a prominent daily newspaper in Winnipeg. On December 9, 1963 the Tribune had an editorial headed, "Leave Our Flag Alone" in which they had this to say:
We already have one. The red ensign under which Canada has lived in peace and war lor three score and ten years is as distinctly Canadian as a flag could be.
No.

I am only quoting authorities and the hon. member can do likewise when his turn comes.
The impatience of the Prime Minister to ram this new flag down the throats of Canadians received this reaction from Bruce West. Writing in the Globe and Mail of June 16, 1964 under the headline "Unhealthy Affair" he had this to say:
X believe that the impatient efforts of many to discard a banner which symbolizes almost a century of our history may be a symptom of something gravely unhealthy in the affairs of Canada.
I also wish to refer to an open letter to the Prime Minister from six prominent Canadian citizens of Winnipeg. Most of them are of ethnic origin, one of them being Salome Holderson, a former member of the legislature of Manitoba and a prominent pedagogue. Among other things these six prominent citizens had this to say to the Prime Minister:
No other country flies the red ensign and It has become known all over the world for half a century as Canada's distinctive flag.
That is another witness I bring forward to support my contention. Let us go further. A distinguished Canadian writer, Dr. Eugene Forsey, had this to say in a letter to the Ottawa Journal of June 13 last:
Everything human, every vestige of our history, everything distinctly Canadian, except a piece of vegetation, has been carefully excluded.
In the same letter he also says:
This government proposes a flag which contains not the slightest reference to any culture whatever, even agriculture.
One is led to ask: Why the hurry? We can surmise that the proponents or champions of the new flag either have no case, cannot make

out a case and therefore would like to bridle discussion and put it through as fast as they can or else they are so sure of their grounds that they are certain the Canadian people will accept the new flag. Time alone will show. I am trying to be reasonable and look at both sides.
The Amherst Daily News of December 29, 1961 contains a report of an interview with the Prime Minister of Canada who was at that time leader of the opposition. He was asked certain questions. I quote:
Question: You say the Liberals are working on a design?
Answer: Oh, there are hundreds of designs, but it would be the responsibility of the government to make up its mind which design it would submit to parliament.
Question: How would you poll the people on this?
Answer: We would poll the people when we have a general election, and if they did not like the idea of a distinctive Canadian flag which cannot be mistaken for that of any other country, they will let us know in no uncertain terms.
That was a pledge made by the leader of the Liberal party who was then hoping to attain victory in an election. He has attained victory. Where is the pledge to poll the Canadian people? Has he forgotten it? In the 1962 and 1963 election campaigns both he and all Liberal candidates made the same pledge when the question came up, that they would give Canada a distinctive Canadian flag.
Diefenbaker too.

Certainly we did, but not the type of flag you are suggesting. But at no time, Mr. Speaker, have I heard it said, or read in any newspaper that the Prime Minister and the Liberal candidates told the Canadian people that when he produced this new distinctive Canadian flag the union jack would be completely eliminated. I should like to know where and when any such promise was made. They did not dare say to the Canadian people that they would eliminate the union jack. That is the reason they kept silent. They just talked about a distinctive Canadian flag. The Canadian people understood they had a distinctive Canadian flag, the red ensign, which had a quasi-legal status, and they interpreted the Liberal promises to mean that if the Liberals ever came into power they would give this distinctive Canadian flag, the red ensign, full and complete legal status in Canada. That is the way the Canadian people interpreted their promises.

No.

I believe that the red ensign has been slandered and libelled in accordance with the same philosophy that Hitler had, that if you keep repeating a lie often enough there will be some people in the country who will eventually accept it as the truth. That is the case about the red ensign. There are two arguments I have heard against it, and I may repeat them. The first is that it is a foreign flag, a British marine flag. The second is that it is not distinctive enough and is not worthy of adoption because it could be mistaken as the flag of some other country.
Hear, hear.

I am glad hon. gentlemen applaud. I want the truth from those who know, those who are the experts here, old politicians and young politicians. I want them to tell me, under what circumstances has the red ensign ever been mistaken as other than the flag of Canada on the field of battle-
Ask Pigeon.
-in international politics, at the United Nations, at NATO, or anywhere here in Canada?
Pigeon will answer you.
I do not mind interruptions but I do not like interrupting other people myself. I hope hon. members will give me a chance to speak.
You asked the question.

Can somebody show me where there was an instance in history during the past 50 years when Canadians whether on the battlefields of France, Africa or Asia were mistaken as some other force than Canadians? Canadians covered themselves with glory under this flag during the last two world wars.
We do not know the views of the majority of Canadians. Let us poll them; let us find out whether there is a majority in favour of a new flag. But I can assure the house that there are a lot of Canadians who feel the red ensign is their flag, the flag which Canadians have dyed an even deeper red in the bloodshed of battle.
The Winnipeg Tribune in an editorial on December 9, 1963 said:
It has flown over decades of national joys and sorrows, triumphs and disappointments. It has become Canada's flag and a glowing part of Canada's heritage.
Is that a true statement? By opposing the amendment proposed by the Leader of the

Canadian Flag
Opposition, the government and those supporting it are denying the Canadian people the right to be asked their views, as was promised by the leader of the Liberal party during an interview at Amherst in 1961, an interview which I have already quoted. If election promises are made to be broken, then the highways and byways of Canada are strewn with political promises broken by the Liberal party. This is just one more of them.
Like a bolt from the blue, like an atom bomb, this flag has been placed before the people of Canada. It took nine days to draft it. It was a hurried job and now the people are confronted with it. What is their reaction?
I will tell you it is a nice reaction.

Hon. members of this
house have received protests from many people, both by letter, telegram and phone call. Whenever we meet with members of the public they express their views vigorously. At the Winnipeg convention the Royal Canadian Legion in no uncertain terms gave the Prime Minister an indication of its attitude towards anything but the red ensign. It is unfortunate that their behaviour was not too polite but, Mr. Speaker, that was the only means they had of showing their displeasure with the high-handed attitude of the government.
The Legion in my area is for a new flag.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Legionnaires had only this method of showing what they wanted. The majority of them want the red ensign. They fought under that flag and it is for them, more than for anyone else in the country, that we owe the freedoms we enjoy today. Is their voice to be ignored? Are they to be derided, laughed and sneered at? That is the impression I am getting from some hon. gentlemen in this house. How can the government of Canada ignore the stand taken by these people?
I have here a petition from the Royal Canadian Legion in Russell in my own constituency, signed by 500 people. This is from Legion branch No. 159 in Russell, sent in by Mr. Loney, and the Canadians who sign it ask that the red ensign be retained. I know the Prime Minister tries to hide behind an alibi that it is the ethnic groups, who have asked for a distinctive Canadian flag. An hon. gentleman on the other side offered the opinion that it was these people who are just dying to

get a new flag but, Mr. Speaker, if you had time to read the names on this petition you would find it includes the names of all nationalities living in Canada. I shall just read two or three of them. First, there is Thomas Jackson, and that is definitely an Anglo-Saxon name; but next to him is Lome Todoruk, and that is a Ukrainian name. Then there is a A. J. Mushumanski. This gentleman is of Polish origin and I know him personally. He signed this petition in favour of the red ensign. Then we have R. S. Clement, which is definitely an Anglo-Saxon name, and then Marshall Johnson. Then we have S. M. Siwak, which is a Ukrainian name.
I know the boys who signed this; and so I ask, why try to produce a smokescreen saying it is the ethnic groups who want a new flag. I would like to know what groups, what organizations and what parts of Canada are pushing the government into this step. I may add that I intend to file this petition with the Clerk, according to the procedure which the Chair outlined to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge).
I also received a resolution from the Royal Canadian Legion branch No. 66, from Crandall, sent in by Mr. Barnes, and another from Legion branch No. 229, Basswood, sent in by Mr. Graham, and a resolution from branch No. 40 Rossburn, sent in by Ed. Harris and Elmer Brown; and a resolution sent by wire from Legion branch No. 8, Virden, sent in by Mr. Nugent, asked that a plebiscite be held on this question.
Is this government the almighty Caesar? Caesar said "Veni, vidi, vici". I say to the government you "venied" and you "vidied" but it will be a long time before you "vici", before you conquer the opinions of the Canadian people. These men of the Canadian Legion are the men who fought for Canada, who figured Canada was worth fighting for.
I want to tell you this. Mr. Speaker. There is a section of the Royal Canadian Legion called the Ukrainian Royal Canadian Legion section. It has eight branches in Canada, with one branch in Winnipeg over 1,000 strong. It held a separate convention at the same time as the Royal Canadian Legion in Winnipeg, and it passed a unanimous resolution in support of the red ensign. They are what you call ethnic people, Ukrainian people, and most of them were volunteers for Canada.
What about the hundreds of other branches of the Legion? I know perfectly well that the supporters of the Liberal party, the hon. members sitting on the government side, have been receiving these protests. I just wonder

how they are answering them. I just wonder how they are going to face these men, what they will tell them when they have deprived them of the opportunity of deciding what Canada should have as its flag. This is evidence I am presenting to the house. I am not relying on my personal feelings.
Everyone is familiar with I.O.D.E., a women's organization which has 29,000 members across Canada. They met at Fredericton a couple of weeks ago and they sent a telegram to the Prime Minister. I wonder what the right hon. gentleman had to say in reply. This is how it read:
We deplore that in this democratic country our government would deprive individual citizens of the right to vote on an issue as vital as the Canadian flag.
Is the government so almighty, is the government so secure, that it intends to ignore this telegram? I go further. I think the Prime Minister or his staff would agree that they have also received a protest from an organization known as the Grand Orange lodge of British America. I am not an Orangeman; I do not agree with some of their views. But this is an organization you cannot sneeze at; you cannot ignore them when they have a membership in 250,000 homes across Canada. What did they ask? In the petition they sent to the Prime Minister they say they support the Canadian Legion on this issue in toto. In other words, they support the Legion's stand on this issue completely. They also say, in their petition:
Be it further resolved that we hereby petition the government to cease further legislation on the flag question until and except the people of Canada by referendum indicate their wishes accordingly.
Some hon. gentlemen look only through the narrow windows of their own constituencies. Because in their own constituencies there is a majority which wants this particular flag, or some other flag, they think the majority of the Canadian people want it. I cannot say that. Nor can any member of this house say with authority or proof that the majority of the Canadian people want either one flag or another.
I have here from the Tribune an article called Viewpoint written by a prominent barrister Mr. Roy St. George Stubbs. He is not a Conservative. I honestly believe he is a supporter of the party which now forms the government. I do not know. I know he is not a Tory, so I cannot be accused of putting forward the opinions of Tories. He is talking about a book written in 1908, and dealing
Canadian Flag
with the Ewart prophesy. I have not time to go into detail, but the article says:
Time has not justified Ewart's prophesy. Were he alive today what would he say about the current proposal to throw 100 years of tradition into the dustbin of history? Can a doubtful gain in national solidarity balance the certain loss in national sentiment?
These are opinions. What about the letters we have all received? I have received them and I know other members have received them in large numbers. The Prime Minister has claimed, it is reported in the press, that he has received thousands and that most of them are in favour of the new design. But I have information that the Leader of the Opposition has received thousands of letters, too, and that most of those are against the new flag. I am glad we are to have a little time to spend on this debate. I hope the Prime Minister will take time to analyse these letters and let us know from what sections of the country they come. Do they all come from one area? I should also like to know from what sections of the country came the letters written to the Leader of the Opposition. We are entitled to know these things and express our opinions.
Bruce West, writing in the Globe and Mail of June 15, called this "an unhealthy affair". Is he correct? He feels, like many Canadians, that impatient efforts to discard the red ensign may be the symbol of an unhealthy state of affairs in Canada and that the day this ensign is discarded some very important threads will be removed from the fabric of this country. He, like so many of us, is afraid that other things which make up what we are will also be discarded. What will be the next to be discarded? Who can say that in five or six years there will not be a movement in Canada to discard this new symbol, too, and put something else in its place. As has been stated even by members on the other side with regard to the red ensign, we have become accustomed to it. Flags do not create unity, said one writer in the Globe and Mail, it is unity which creates flags. Let us have unity first. Let us show we have a nation.
In closing I say this: If anything, the flag resolution before us creates disunity. It has led to argument all over the country. I was in my constituency about a week ago and I would hate to repeat some of the things which were said about the Prime Minister because he had proposed this new flag. I hate to read some of the letters which refer to the Prime Minister and in which the writers attempt

Canadian Flag
to say in not very polite terms what they think of him for proposing this new design. This is an important issue, but we are not to have a plebiscite. If members on the other side think they have a mandate, I should like to know from whom. If supporters of the government had told the Canadian people that the Canadian flag they intended to propose was going to eliminate the union jack then, I would say, they had a mandate. But who ever made that statement? Did the Prime Minister make it? Did any member of the Liberal cabinet make it? Did any of the others who are supporting this resolution, probably not through conviction-this resolution designed to get rid of the symbol we call the red ensign?
If this legislation is important, why rush it through? Why must the Prime Minister say we will not get a summer recess before we finish this debate? Everything else must stop but he intends to continue this debate. Does he wish to wear us out? If this is important legislation we should be given time to debate it. I should like to hear members opposite tell us who is backing them on this issue? Don't give us history about Sir John Macdonald. Don't read us something out of books 150 years old. Tell us what organizations are supporting you. I will listen carefully to the speeches hon. members opposite have to make on this subject and I know the Canadian people will be listening, too. I am giving the house evidence. I have referred to petitions. If all those organizations are added together they amount to more than a million people.
How?

Well, there are a quarter
of a million Legion members. There are a quarter of a million Orangemen. Then there are the members of I.O.D.E. and the ethnic groups.
We want to know why there should be this rush. If the government has a good case for introducing this new symbol they need not be afraid of stepping out and telling the house and the country why. They need not be afraid of protracted debate. Are you taking it for granted just because the government think they can muster up a majority in the house, and knowing that the Canadian people, once an enactment passes the house-
Order, please. Would the hon. member desist for a moment.
