AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.

And of the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.

Mr. Speaker, there is some difficulty in resuming an interrupted speech, with eight or nine minutes more to go, in getting back into high gear and into the same mood. I could have completed my remarks in that time because I had only one other point to bring to the attention of the house, namely that the government must be uncertain whether the new flag with the three maple leaves represents truly just what we are, because there is another resolution on the order paper for the adoption of a second flag, namely the union jack. I am not against the union jack. I am in favour of it because the union jack is the flag of the United Kingdom and, I might add, not a flag established under any statute. It has become the flag of the United Kingdom by usage or custom and it is dear to that nation of the commonwealth. Whether the government is trying to borrow it or steal it I am unable to understand.
Let me point out that the union jack is the flag of the land of origin of a lot of people in this nation, while the red ensign is the flag that we are accustomed to. It has flown amongst us, it is a part of our heritage and it has on it the Canadian coat of arms. If parliament were to go so far as to adopt two flags I can well envisage that either one or the other might be flown in different parts of Canada. Just imagine the impression that would make on foreigners visiting this country if they saw one flag flown in one part of Canada and another flag flown in another part of Canada. Would they not come to the conclusion that we are a divided nation, that we are not one Canada but two Canadas or two nations? If that is what the government has in mind they might as well spell it out.
At the beginning of my speech I said that my views on this matter are known to all. I come from the old school, Mr. Speaker. I can still sing: There'll always be an England as long as Scotland stands. I can still sing: In days of yore from Britain's shore, and so on and so forth. But I am prepared to go along with the times, and if there are changes that we must make on the flag that is dear to many Canadians I for one would be prepared to make those changes, add something to the red ensign to give some indication of our second founding race and thus satisfy all in that way. But let us retain our heritage. Let us retain the symbols of the past.
Canadian Flag
Everyone, Mr. Speaker, whether a lawyer by profession or an ordinary individual, at one time or another has been in court and anyone who is a plaintiff or appellant must make out a case. In this instance the government is the appellant. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is the main spokesman for those who appeal for a new distinctive flag. They must make out a case. Pointing to history or heraldic symbols is not going to satisfy Canadians. As I said before the dinner recess, the government must show that they have a mandate. They must show who are behind the new flag. They must show the reasons for it.
We are the respondents, Mr. Speaker, and as one of the respondents or defendants I have called witnesses. My witnesses have been the Legion, the I.O.D.E., the Orangemen, the ethnic groups and many others. I challenge the government to produce its witnesses. I challenge the government to submit this resolution to a special committee of the house and give people who have various ideas for or against the red ensign or the new flag the opportunity to make out a case. I feel that so far no member of the government, no supporter of the new design, has made out a case for the new flag.
I know that some eastern newspapers have been very critical of my stand with regard to the flag. But I want to say to all concerned that I, and those others of my race, were invited to come to this country. We came of our own free will. We came here not to ruin that which was built by the founding races but to continue the building of that great structure, one great Canada. We came here to put our shoulders together with the shoulders of the French and the British, and shoulder to shoulder to march forward to a unity of one Canada, not two Canadas, three Canadas or anything else.
We are just as proud of our heritage and love our language just as much as English or French Canadians love theirs, but at the same time we are prepared to give that which is necessary to make up one great Canadian nation such as was envisaged by the fathers of confederation.
I as a Ukrainian am proud of the fact that this year the Ukrainians in Canada and the United States, as you may have seen on television last week, unveiled another monument to Taras Shevchenko the freedom fighter of the Ukrainian race. We are proud of this man who gave so much in the cause of freedom. We are proud to celebrate the 150th anniversary of his birth. He fought for the freedom of all people, for the freedom of all

Business of the House Ukrainians. We are hurt that 40 million of our people are still behind the iron curtain but I, and those like me, are giving what we can here in Canada. We are passing this on to our children and we know that our children's children will do likewise.
I appeal for unity, but at the same time there is no use appealing for unity and not doing anything about it. We are happy to live in this nation. Let us make it great. If anyone has created a disturbance, if anyone has given rise to the emotional struggle that is going on in Canada today, it is the right hon. Prime Minister. If he thinks this flag is necessary above all, then he will be the one who will suffer the consequences when the people of Canada have a chance to make their wishes known.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask unanimous consent to revert to motions to make a statement on the business of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, it may be helpful if I review future business for the house as it appears to be after the meetings of the house leaders of the various parties yesterday and today. Those meetings did not accomplish everything that it was hoped they might do, but they were friendly and constructive meetings. I believe some progress was made, and I hope that progress is a happy augury for future progress. But as there was no agreement at this stage, at least on the order of business for July, I think it would be wise if I put the program of the government to the house in this way, especially as this might correct some inaccurate reports which have been circulating as to what the government might propose.
I would first, Mr. Speaker, like to remind the house that a detailed statement on business was laid before this chamber on June 3, nearly a month ago, and since that time we have been following the priorities given to parliament at that time. The first four items on that priority list of June 3 have now been dealt with: (1) the approval of the Columbia treaty; (2) the national housing legislation; (3) the farm credit extension bill and (4) the constitutional amendment to provide for supplementary benefits in our pension legislation.
Since that statement of June 3 we have introduced into the house a resolution which


the house is now considering, the flag resolution. We interrupted that resolution, as on June 3 we told the house we might have to do, in order to secure agreement on the constitutional amendment which I have mentioned, and to ask for interim supply. These two items have now been completed.
The government has been urged to postpone the flag resolution, as it is obstructing other legislation and as it is, as we all admit, a measure which is controversial and arouses deep and genuine emotions. So far as obstructing other legislation is concerned, I think it is quite clear that there never will be a time when this flag issue, which is an issue of vital national importance, will not be controversial and will not interfere with other legislative proposals to which some hon. members would, for various reasons, wish to give priority over it. So, whenever this resolution would be introduced in the house there would be that difficulty.
Therefore the government feels that the flag issue should be proceeded with. It is our hope that, with three days debate having already taken place, the house might be in a position to make at least a decision on the amendment to the resolution by the end of this week. However I am not urging here any limit of any kind to a discussion of a matter of such importance. On the other hand, we do not wish a prolonged debate on this issue to postpone decisions on certain other matters which are ready for decision and which decision, I think, should be taken as early in July as possible, and at least certainly during the month of July, and the meetings that have been held and the consideration given to this matter have been influenced by the sincere desire to reconcile these two considerations.
In an effort to do that, I propose for the government the following program for action by the house before we take a summer recess. On Thursday we shall interrupt the flag resolution debate to introduce a resolution on the youth allowances bill, and I understand there has been unanimous consent among the house leaders that there should be no debate on that resolution and that it should go through. I appreciate that attitude. The bill would then be given first reading and circulated. Then on Thursday and Friday we would continue with the flag resolutions.
Then we propose that the national defence bill, which has already been given a great deal of attention, should be considered next Monday, July 6, and if the house comes to a decision on that bill we would proceed to

the consideration of the youth allowances bill and continue with that legislation until it is completed. Perhaps I can express the hope that that would not take too long, because we are all in agreement on the principle ot that bill.
Then we would go from the youth allowances bill to the fiscal arrangements bill which is very important, indeed as important to the provinces as it is to us. It is a matter of some urgency that we give consideration to it. That bill will be followed by the bill for the 12 mile jurisdictional zone, which I would hope would not take too long as it has already been discussed in the house and in committee. The house would then, after the 12 mile zone bill, be asked to consider the student loans bill. I understand there is agreement that the resolution covering that measure would be passed without discussion too, so that the bill could be circulated. Then .provision will be made during the first half of July for further interim supply since we asked for, and received, only one month's supply at our last request. Then I think at least two Fridays during the month of July should be devoted to estimates.
If this legislative program can be completed by July 22 or 23-I do not know whether it can be or not, but if it could be, and I would hope that perhaps it could be- we would have the rest of the month, that is seven or eight days more, to deal with the flag resolutions. In any event, when the matters I have mentioned are dealt with, we shall return to the flag resolutions and the debate on those resolutions would be continued until a decision is reached on them.
Oh, oh.

We would not, however, ask the house before a summer recess to consider the resolution on the national anthem or the royal anthem.
It will be seen, Mr. Speaker, from the timetable I have suggested to the house, one which will no doubt be given further consideration by the house leaders, that it is not possible to predict with any certainty the date of a summer adjournment. I was asked to submit a target date. The target date I should like to submit is the end of July. If we meet that target date it would be our desire and, I think, the desire of all members of the house, for parliament to recess until the middle of September.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We have had an announcement by the Prime Minister with regard to the busi-
Business of the House ness of the house. I noticed that he indicated that the house has accomplished quite a lot during the month of June, as he listed the various items which he had spoken about on June 3 and which have already been passed. I noted that five items of legislation, most of which we have been asking the government to put forward, will be considered by the house next week and we think this is a sensible thing to do, because we believe the measures dealing with youth allowances and student loans in particular should have been brought up earlier than this.
As a party we are prepared to assist the government in passing these legislative items next week, and if the bills are carefully drawn and if, after subjecting them to careful scrutiny, they are found to be in order, I do not see any particular reason why there should be any great delay in passing those measures. If they are for the good of the country we will pass them. If there are items in any of these measures with which we are not in agreement we shall state our disagreement, as is our duty and obligation as an opposition.
I noted the Prime Minister said there would be two Fridays in July devoted to the consideration of the main estimates. I record a very strong objection to that limitation of time spent on main estimates. The main estimates constitute the spending program of the government and this spending program should be very carefully examined by the House of Commons. In sessions in the past it was normal for main estimates to be considered on Thursdays and Fridays of each week. That has not been the case this session and the main estimates are going to be piled up until the close of the session some time in the fall. I think that is not a good arrangement. I certainly would like to enter a very strong objection to the failure to deal with main estimates. This spending program of the government requires the same type of examination as the tax program of the government set out in the budget.
The Prime Minister went on to say that after the completion of the legislative items he mentioned we would consider interim supply, and if that were passed by July 22 or 23 we would have seven or eight days left for the flag debate. He then came to the crux of the matter. He said that the session would continue-he was referring to the flag resolutions-"until a decision is reached on them". That is very definite. That tells us exactly the position we are in. To speak of a target date of July 31 can be quite

Business of the House meaningless unless the opposition bows to the will of the government because, in effect, the Prime Minister is saying: You will get a summer recess only when you have reached a decision with regard to the flag.
So we know now exactly what our position is. It is quite clear that no summer recess was envisaged by the Prime Minister unless the opposition abdicated its position in this house. We are rather pleased that the situation has now been so clearly stated and that we know exactly what was in the Prime Minister's mind when the motion was put forward the other day to extend the hours of sitting. The situation is simply this, Mr. Speaker: As the official opposition we are prepared to co-operate to the fullest extent on this matter of legislation which has been brought to our attention and pass it without unusual delay, subject as I said to careful scrutiny. Having done that, then to have a club held over our heads-and this is what it amounts to-by the statement "no end to this particular session until a decision on the flag is reached", is a somewhat unusual position for a government to take. But now we know clearly the government's stand, and there will be no misunderstanding in this house as to the intention of the government because it has been clearly set before us: no summer recess unless the opposition bows to the government with regard to the flag.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the action of the Prime Minister in making this statement to the house as to the intention of the government with respect to business for the next few weeks. I think it is also fair to say that, now we have had a couple of meetings of the house leaders, it is well to have the results of our negotiations up to this point out in the open.
I want to say that we appreciate the position the government has taken in altering to some extent its stand of last week by agreeing to interrupt the debate on the flag to deal with these five or six important items. We think this is the position the government should have taken all along. At any rate, we commend the government for now having taken this position and we feel, as do members of other parties in the house, that perhaps we could best show our appreciation by expediting the passing of these five or six items when they come before us. The Prime Minister is perfectly correct in stating that the spokesmen for all parties agreed that there need be no debate what-


soever at the resolution stage of the youth allowance measure or on the resolution stage of the student loans legislation. I think there is also a disposition on the part of the house leaders to look at the other measures when we have the actual bills before us to ascertain whether there are steps we could take to shorten debate on these measures at various stages. I do think it does not hurt to take a moment or two to emphasize that we have made progress in the meetings which we had yesterday and today.
Before leaving this phase of my brief remarks may I say I have something in common with my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). I too have a protest which I want to lodge. It is not the same protest but it is one which I lodge even more vigorously than the one he has stated. I protest on behalf of the members of this party at the fact that the Canada pension plan is not included in the items to be dealt with before we return to the flag debate. It was always our understanding that the Canada pension plan debate could not be concluded in what might be called the first part of the session, but we understood that serious efforts would be made to get it past second reading and referred to the special committee which is to study the measure.
I want to say that I regard this further delay with respect to the Canada pension plan as ominous. All the members of the house are aware of the delays which have already taken place with respect to this matter since this parliament began. Each time the Canada pension plan has been proposed we have been assured that we were going through with it, but always there is a delay. I can now see that when we are meeting this fall trying to wind up the business before Christmas or whenever this session ends we will have some more of these bargaining sessions. Matters like redistribution, the Canada pension plan, the railway legislation and other matters will be before us and we will go through the same business that we have been through scores of times. We will have to agree that something has to be dropped. Again, my fear is that it will be the Canada pension plan which will be put aside; and if this goes on many more times there is no stating what might happen. I am delighted to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) shaking his head from right to left; I hope it was in response to what I have just said. I would remind him that the same kind of assurance has been given before, but at any rate for the moment, like the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I register

my protest that the Canada pension plan is not included among the items to be dealt with before we return to the debate on the flag.
Now, with respect to these five items on which we have reached agreement at the meetings of the house leaders, I should like to say that I think the suggested date of July 23 is a little too far off. I think we can do these five items several days ahead of July 23. Let us just look at them. There is the national defence bill which we almost finished last night. Surely another few hours will dispose of it. With regard to the youth allowance measure which extends family allowances to 16 and 17 year olds, we all agree with it and surely that should not take very long. The federal-provincial fiscal relations and arrangements legislation might take a little time; we will not know how long until we see the bill, but even so it should not take very long. The student loans legislation ought to go through as quick as a flash. The 12 mile fishing zone legislation is still before the committee on marine and fisheries, but if the committee reaches agreement on the terms of the bill it should not take very long in the house. So with respect to those five items- I have named them all but interim supply- I do not think it would be unreasonable to suggest they could be done in a week, leaving a few days if we need them for interim supply.
We all know the facts of life, and we all know when we get to interim supply that the length of time spent will depend on the strategy of the various parties in the house; it will depend on what might have happened in the meantime. All sorts of things can take place. But I am taking these few moments deliberately to emphasize the extent to which we reached agreement at the meetings of the house leaders. We have agreed that these five items of legislation are important, that we are satisfied with them subject to seeing the details of some of the legislation, and that we can get them through quickly.
The point I wish to make in setting this phase of our work off against the debate on the flag is this. I urge that we leave until we have got through the first five pieces of legislation any argument, discussion, dogfight or what-have-you over time to be spent discussing the flag. I think it would be good for parliament to have the accomplishment of passing five or six pieces of legislation in a week or so, and when that is done to continue to hold our meetings of house leaders when perhaps we can resolve what may be an impasse when the time comes. But let that anticipated impasse not interfere with our doing 20220-312J
Business of the House
an effective piece of work now. I am not denying the fact that the impasse will be there when we reach it. The government is saying that it wants the flag resolution put through before there is a recess. The official opposition regards that as a club. We feel that there should be a recess, not because we want a holiday but because we think it would be good for parliament if we saw a little less of each other for a couple of weeks and came back here fresh. We think that we would do better service in this way to the people of Canada. But I suggest that this whole question of trying to resolve this impasse over the flag should not be one which is allowed to impede our work on student loans or on youth allowances or on these other pieces of legislation. Let us deal with them on their merits; let us do a good job; and maybe the practice of getting some pieces of legislation through in short order will have a contagious effect and we will go on doing it.
I have been delighted, Mr. Speaker, despite any differences which we have had, with the progress achieved at our meetings yesterday and today. I think it has been unfortunate that there have been reports about these meetings which were not entirely accurate. Therefore it was a good idea for the Prime Minister to make the statement he did tonight, and if we can emphasize the measure of agreement which we achieve and face up to the fact that the people of Canada want us to get some work done, I think we can move along. Therefore my plea is that we get along with these five pieces of legislation which are agreed upon and then see if we cannot go on and keep up the good work.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to be very brief. I should like to suggest that in making his statement I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) minimized the results of the meetings which were held between the house leaders. I do not think that was intentional, but I do believe that we made a little greater progress than was indicated in the statement he made. I felt that there were very worth-while results and I think we are encouraged to keep working at the job of trying to expedite the business of the house. However, we do appreciate the statement the Prime Minister has made tonight to clarify the situation as far as the government is concerned.
Thinking back over these past weeks since the session started, I do not think we have anything to brag about as far as conducting the business of the nation is concerned. In

Business of the House spite of the fact that there has been a number of items passed I think we could have done a good deal more than we have done up to the present time. We also appreciate the fact that the government has moved to a certain degree as far as the controversial flag resolution is concerned and is providing an opportunity for the dispatch of a number of other items which are of vital interest to the country.
I am not going to enumerate them again because they have been enumerated several times tonight. As far as we are concerned, we feel it is a good thing that we give our attention specifically to these matters of business that are of vital concern and have some degree of urgency in them, so that those affected will be able to plan for future days. As I have said, we intend to give our complete support to the passage of these particular measures.
I just wish to say, however, that I am disappointed in the position the government is still taking-and the Prime Minister indicated this tonight-as far as the resolutions on the flag are concerned. We felt that with the passage of a number of other items, this was one that was not of such tremendous urgency that it would be used to decide whether or not there was going to be a recess of parliament for the summer. However, this has been made abundantly clear tonight, and the question that is in our minds is this: What is going to happen if and when an irresistible force meets an immovable object? Possibly we will have to wait until that time comes to see just what does happen. But I do think it is unfortunate that this adamant position is being maintained in the face of the present situation. I am not going to debate it now, because the debate on the flag is under way and we will have an opportunity then. As I have said, we want to get ahead with the business of the nation, and we will face these things as and when the situation arises.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a few words to say on behalf of our group about the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). We are quite satisfied with the order of business he announced, particularly as regard the family allowances legislation and student allowances.
People had already asked us for information on those allowances, but we reserved our answers, hoping from week to week that the government might bring forward a bill

so that next year students would know where they stood. We are quite happy to learn that the discussion on that bill will begin this week.
We earnestly call for the support of all opposition parties so that this work can be completed within two days. In fact, most of us agree on those pieces of legislation.
It is said that most hon. members do not even wish to discuss those measures, but are ready to simply pass them.
However, there may still be some objections. I think they will result in an extension of debates, rather than an attack against the principle of those measures and this, in order to postpone that much longer resumption of the discussion on the flag issue.
We commend the government for having made concessions and we also praise the leaders who attended the meeting and who made use of all their talents and their goodwill to reach an agreement.
When all that urgent legislation has been passed, let us get on with the flag debate and settle the question once and for all.
We have been discussing this issue for 40 years and it is high time we are done with it. Let each member vote according to his own feelings so that the people of Canada may see that their parliament still has some sense of responsibility and that it no longer spends its time in futile discussions, as it did last week when members acted like 10-year olds.
Let us discuss each piece of legislation and then take the vote. Let us stop arguing for nothing and let us take the vote. Let us get on with our program so that we may finally examine the flag resolution.
Here I want to congratulate the Prime Minister for his steadfastness. To some people, this is the sword of Damocles or cloture, the French word for fence. But a fence along a road is a guide line, not a prison. What the Prime Minister gave this evening was an indication, a firm invitation.
I hope the official opposition will not hold up indefinitely the business of the house. It often resorts to systematic obstruction which I find unacceptable in parliamentary procedure and which should not exist. When everybody has expressed his views, let us vote once and for all. Those who favour the adoption of a distinctive flag will vote for it, and the question will be settled. If the distinctive flag is rejected by the majority of members, that will be just too bad. It does not matter, the majority will decide, because in democratic countries it is still up to the majority to decide.

I congratulate the government about the decision it has just taken and I can assure it of our full support both as regards this attitude and the adoption of the flag.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The house will now resume the business that was interrupted by reverting to motions.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a Held of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And of the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.

Mr. Speaker, the suggestion has been made during the course of this debate outside of the house itself that the course of action being advocated in the matter of national symbols represents our doing something new and rejecting something that is old. I do not subscribe to this interpretation of this course of action. The government, it seems to me, is asking that this parliament proclaim as the national flag a distinctive Canadian symbol that has in one form or another existed in this country for 100 years or so and has in fact been part of our heritage. In the same subject matter of national symbols we are also being asked to give recognition to those symbols of the commonwealth and our monarchical ties. We are, as it were, being asked to decide formally and once and for all that we recognize in this particular way Canada's status as an independent nation, but an independent nation within the British commonwealth.
Canada has become such a nation over the years, not by revolution, not by sudden change or sudden means but by a gradual, an evolutionary process. At each stage of this evolutionary development voices of resistance have raised themselves because it was feared that Canada was breaking its ties with the mother country and moving in a direction inconsistent with that of a former British possession. In actual fact I submit that the opposite is the case. This evolutionary development of ours
Canadian Flag
toward nationhood was in fact, and is, done in a most British way. We might say that as a nation we have approached the problems of our nationhood more British than the British themselves. In all times and in all examples we have followed, as it were, due process of law. Great national debate preceded all these formal changes. I will not list them but I know they are familiar to all members. As these changes were wrought in Canada's march to nationhood, debate was the order of the day and the great forum for these debates was here in parliament, this parliament modelled after the mother of parliaments. The fathers of confederation, it seems to me, had as their goal a united and a strong nation on this North American continent, but a nation that would be governed according to those institutions, customs and traditions which were British, largely, in origin; a nation that would be monarchical rather than republican-but a nation, nevertheless, independent and united.
Were we not so cognizant of these British uses and traditions, perhaps we would have followed a different course on the road toward nationhood. Perhaps we would have attempted to settle our problems in what, to me, would have seemed to be a logical, clear cut way, but would have, in fact, represented our approach to these things in one fell swoop. In so doing, we would not be approaching them in the British way and in a way that would have been in keeping with our traditions; we would not be in keeping with our past.
We have moved into the future, not in bold steps that might have threatened our affection for the past, but instead we have moved slowly in a way characteristic, perhaps, of this nation; in compromise, in a pragmatic way. In doing so, in adopting compromise and pragmatism, we have paid a great tribute to the country to which so many of us owe so much. This pragmatism of which I speak is so much a part of our heritage; it is one of the gifts that England has given us. Not all or even a majority of the Canadian people today are of British origin, yet all Canada notes with pride the customs and traditions that are tied to this association. There is our system of government, parliamentary democracy, rather than republicanism. This is something which sets us apart from our neighbour to the south. It is something which is revered by all Canadians. It consists of something British and also something Canadian.

Canadian Flag
A few moments ago I referred to the existing Canadian personality as pragmatic, and compared it to being something British, because this is almost Britain's stock in trade in dealing with her own problems and world problems. Today we are asked to take one more step-true it is only a formal step-on the road to true and complete national sovereignty in form as well as in fact. I think that we should be asked to do this in a way most consistent with our Canadian heritage and tradition. We are now asked to declare a distinctive Canadian flag, not something new that is the design or the whim of some patriot. We are asked to declare as the flag of Canada a symbol which, as I suggested earlier, has been with us for 100 years or more. It is, you might say, in that sense a flag that is both old and new. We are being asked also for the first time to give recognition to certain commonwealth symbols which will be discussed, 1 presume at another time.
The suggestion has been made we should approach this problem of our national symbols in another way. The suggestion has been made that a plebiscite should be taken. If we are to follow that course of action we would be flying in the face of British parliamentary democracy. I am unaltered in my opposition to a government shirking its responsibilities and turning to republican innuendos in the form of government plebiscite. The mother of parliaments, in its wisdom throughout the years, has not seen fit to so degrade itself. However, I regret to say this parliament has not adopted at all times a similarly wise course.
However, as somebody has suggested, perhaps that was before Newfoundland entered confederation. While I am on that subject of Newfoundland and confederation for a moment, I was reminded before I got to my feet that almost 200 years ago, when Canada was in great peril, a little band of Newfoundlanders came up to Quebec and helped to turn back the Americans. Fifteen years ago Newfoundland was taken into Canada to help with her glorious future. We decided at that time we should insure that future, once and for all, so that we would not have to run back and forth.
After that slight diversion, I might say that deciding this matter of national symbols through debate in this House of Commons is the British way. It is consistent with our traditions. I am grateful, and I congratulate the government for not giving in to the temptation that we do something foreign to our traditions and adopt a republican course
[Mr. Cashin.l
of action. I should like to congratulate all members who have taken part in this debate, particularly the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson). I believe he showed a true understanding of tradition, at least in the context of the realities of our present age. I think he showed the example of the beauty and virtue of tradition which does not, of itself, become our mistress but gives us a guide line for future action. I wish more people could have been in the house at that time to hear a very worthy address.
The province, part of which I have had the privilege of representing for some year or so in this house, is new to the sovereign nation of Canada. Our ties with Britain have been similar, but perhaps somewhat closer than those of Canada. I feel sure that Newfoundlanders who, some 15 years ago after considerably heated debate decided to tie their destiny with that of Canada, realized they would be called upon to make contributions to the future of this country. It seems to me, as a Newfoundlander and, in a sense a new Canadian, it would be a more important thing for Canada to produce truly distinctive symbols of its own, yet at the same time, in the truly Canadian tradition, retain those things of our past for which we have so much genuine affection and loyalty. The course of action in this regard followed by this government, I think is one that will be hailed in years to come as being the course of action advocated by neither one side nor the other, but one truly consistent with our traditions and our heritage; a course of action that will, I think, serve well the purpose of national unity.

Mr. Speaker, there was a time when I thought there would not be very much discussion on the resolution before us at the moment. Now, however, I And that there has been much said and we probably can look forward to much more being said. In addition to that, a great deal of time of this house will be taken. The reason for this, I think, is apparent from the resolution itself which was brought before this house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) . It refers to the fact that the government be authorized to take such steps as are necessary. The government should be authorized by whom? This is the question, not only in my mind, not only in the minds of many others in this house, but in the minds of many people across this country. I intend to deal with that later.
These are the questions being asked, Mr. Speaker. Why is this necessary? We in this

house, indeed the people of Canada, were led to believe or my impression was that we were led to believe this question would not be that the government be authorized, but that parliament would have a free vote. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that many people are not aware what is involved in a free vote. When they hear the words "free vote" they take them literally as meaning that the members of the House of Commons and the other place may vote in the way their consciences direct, particularly in the case of an issue of conscience, an emotional issue, as the flag resolution has been described so many times. It is an issue of the type on which one could very well expect to have a free vote.
There are many reasons why this should be so, and with the indulgence of the house I shall bring some of them forward later. Why should I, not having any intention previously of speaking, be standing here taking the time of the house to put forward my own views and those of my constituents? Why is this necessary? In an emotional issue of this kind, an issue of conscience, I feel that I must express my views and the views of my constituents whereas if there had been going to be a free vote my position might have been different. It follows, therefore, that at this time I am delegated to bring forward the views of different factions, different groups, different individuals in my constituency. This is necessary because the Prime Minister, after having first given the strong impression indirectly, if not directly, that there would be a free vote on this highly contentious and emotional issue, said latterly that the government would stand or fall on the issue. Some people may have different ideas about the interpretation of statements like that, but to me it simply means that this issue has now become a political one.
A political flag.

This is the unavoidable result now, no matter what flag is adopted. Certainly if the flag outlined in the resolution is adopted it will be a political flag as well. If that should happen we will then have a flag that is not identified as a distinctive Canadian flag. It will be identified then as a political flag, and this may be good, bad or indifferent. Someone else will have to judge. Not only will it be identified as a political flag but it will also be identified with a certain person and a certain political party.
I deplore this attitude, Mr. Speaker. I had genuinely and sincerely hoped that parliament would have a free vote, and I think
Canadian Flag
there are many in this party who feel the same way. There may also be some in other parties. Certainly there would have been very little objection if a free vote had been allowed. There came a time, however, when the Prime Minister realized that this would not bring to culmination what he had in mind.
A lot has been said about certain types of training, and from many years of schooling and experience I have had the impression, and still have, that a democratic leader in the true sense is the servant of the wishes of the people in a democracy. This resolution is not one brought forward by a democratic leader or government. How can it be, Mr. Speaker, when we are told that this will be it? Many times in the last few weeks we have been told that this will be it, like it or not, even to the point of suspending consideration of other legislation. We were told this to all intents and purposes only 15 minutes ago in the house. All other legislation will be put aside after a certain point is reached.
The same old gang.

I hear comments about the same old bunch. We were told by the Prime Minister that after a certain point nothing else would be done in this session of parliament until the flag resolution was disposed of. As I said before, this is not my idea of a democratic leader or a democratic government. It sounds much more like a dictatorship. I had another word on the tip of my tongue. We should not have to be subjected to this procedure, Mr. Speaker. As has been mentioned before, there is a great deal of evidence that the proposed design is not as popular as some people think it is. I, like every other member of the house, can quote many prayers and petitions, and read letters, but there is something I would like to read before my time runs out. It is a summary of what the constituency of Lethbridge expects me to bring forth to this house, and it is this: Canadians generally are agreed or may agree to having a distinctive Canadian flag. They may agree upon this by themselves, maybe even through parliament alone, but as I expressed a few moments earlier we have been given to understand very clearly and distinctly that this will not be possible.
It has now become a political issue and, when it becomes a political issue, then the flag adopted will become a political flag and will be associated politically with certain people and with a certain political party. I definitely want to leave this thought with the house, that I cannot agree that any flag which

Canadian Flag
has this kind of association can be a distinctive Canadian flag regardless of the desire to have one.
The representations I have had from the constituency of Lethbridge point out to me that there is a great majority who strongly insist that the Canadian ensign be retained, or something very near to it. There are others who would go a little further but who would still retain much, if not all of the ensign.
This brings forth mention of a new design. I know how hopeless it is for me as a backbencher, as a member of the official opposition, to present the design of a flag, but later in my speech I would like to make a suggestion that has been prompted by all the representations I have received from those who have taken the trouble to make their wishes known to me.
There are some who would like the proposed flag, and there are more who would prefer a single maple leaf design. As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I am not able to summarize the representations I have received from my constituency, but I am delegated more or less to the House of Commons to present the wishes of my constituency, and this I am doing. I have pointed out that there is a great majority who strongly think we should have the ensign. I have pointed out another majority, slightly less, who would be willing to modify that flag but still retain certain parts of it. I have pointed out that there are those in my constituency who favour the flag described in the resolution, and I have pointed out that there are those who favour the design of a single maple leaf. This brings one to realize that the amendment to the resolution is very necessary. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I support the amendment. When the Prime Minister and the government take the stand they do, then I see no other way by which the Canadian people can be satisfied on the design of a distinctive Canadian flag but through being given the opportunity to express their wishes.
My constituency may not coincide in its views with other constituencies, but it is a fairly average constituency. We talk about the wishes, the tendencies or the preferences of constituencies for a distinctive Canadian flag, but according to the cross-Canada newspaper poll, which I watched very closely, the Lethbridge Herald, a newspaper circulating in the general area from which I come, showed a greater percentage of voters in favour of the new design than did the newspaper circulating in Sherbrooke, Quebec.
[Mr. Gundlock.l
There must be a significance in this. It shows that the flag design is not as popular in certain parts of the country as a lot of people would like to have us believe. According to the newspaper poll Lethbridge, Alberta, had a greater percentage of people in favour of the proposed flag than Sherbrooke, Quebec.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, I very seldom take up much time of the house, but there is something that has bothered me on this issue. I have thought it should not be allowed to pass unchallenged. I know that being a new and very inexperienced member I am treading on dangerous ground, but-

I rise on a point of order. I may be mistaken, but I think the hon. member mentioned my riding a moment ago. He said there were more people in his riding in favour of the new flag than there were in my riding, and I think that is not correct.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Would the hon. member kindly resume his seat. I can tell the hon. member that that is not a point of order. It is a matter of debate and the hon. member will have an opportunity to rectify the facts, if he thinks they are not correct, when he takes part in the debate.

Without referring directly to anything I mentioned a while ago I would have no objection whatsoever to repeating what I said. According to my knowledge of recent newspaper polls, they pointed out at a certain point that in my area percentagewise there were more people in favour of the flag design in this resolution before us than were reported as being in favour of it in Sherbrooke, Quebec. There is no insinuation there, whatsoever. I was only pointing out that probably some of us get carried away a little. I was surprised, as a matter of fact, though I do not put any credence in these polls. I mentioned them for whatever they are worth. President Truman has a very good description of polls, one which I do not think I can use here. He did not use it in his chamber and I am sure you would disallow it here, Mr. Speaker. That is all I said. There was certainly nothing personal about it.
But there is something to which I take exception, though it may not refer directly to either this resolution or the amendment. Certain members in particular of this house have made statements with which I cannot agree, and I would quote in this regard the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). At page 4757 of Hansard he is reported as saying:

Let us put s stop to our discussion and settle the matter of the flag right now.
I see the hon. member for Villeneuve is not in his seat. I wish he were. In one way I am glad he is not, though, because I realize he is a much more able debater than I am on the floor of this house. Nevertheless, this is what he said:
Let us put a stop to our discussion and settle the matter of the flag right now.
Well, all hon. members, including the Prime Minister, know that this is not possible. He went on to say:
The cleavage between these two racial groups of Canada is getting even worse.
This is a member of parliament speaking -a responsible man uttering words such as these. The hon. member used those very words:
As I said yesterday, and I repeat it today, the cleavage between the two racial groups of Canada is getting even worse and I hold the Leader of the Opposition responsible for this situation.
As I said before, I take exception to this, and I challenge this statement. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, just where and how can one draw this line between two races in Canada? I have a colleague who usually sits here in front of me. This evening he is sitting just over there. Is he a man of a different race from mine? Is the hon. member I have just quoted, the hon. member for Villeneuve, a man from a different race? I say no, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear.

Statements such as that have gone unchallenged in this house so many times that I feel it is necessary to bring this point up, though I realize it may not be connected directly with ths resolution or with the amendment. But just for a moment I should like to remind some of my hon. friends-and if I may put it in the words of the hon. member for Villeneuve, those of the other race-that there are a lot of people concerned with their welfare, probably much more concerned than some of those who speak so much and so loudly in this place.
I mean this honestly and sincerely, Mr. Speaker. When I say we are concerned about this question, I can support my contention. As a matter of fact I can bring up my campaign material from my last campaign, from my previous campaign and from my first campaign. Throughout we campaigned on government policy. Particularly, we campaigned in the west on the basis of
Canadian Flag
certain policies set out by the former minister of agriculture my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton). Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that is a purely selfish attitude for Canadians to take? Do you think that sort of thing is brought on by people of another race? I hope that when the hon. member is in his place he will bring my attention back to this at some future date. There is more I would like to say about this particular matter, Mr. Speaker, but I shall not do so at the moment.
There is another point along the same line. Ministers of the present government are often quoted in the press. I wish to refer to a statement made by a very respected minister-as a matter of fact, one for whom I personally have a great deal of respect-and I might say this remark is attributed to him in a press release. This newspaper article bears the heading "No answer for Quebec, Favreau says". I would like to read certain portions of it:
An honest man cannot give a precise answer to the question: What does Quebec want? justice minister Guy Favreau told a Liberal party rally here on Saturday.
Even if the man were a mind reader with the agility of a modern computer his answer would be long, tedious and inconclusive, Mr. Favreau said.
If I digress for a moment from the quotation, Mr. Speaker, as I was saying earlier, I do not think these things are all as bad as some people would like us to believe. If I may put it this way, we in the west do not consider ourselves a different race from those in Quebec.
Hear, hear.

We in the west-perhaps I should say "I", but I will say "we"-do not consider Canada selfishly; we do not think we can get along without them. I wish I had more time, Mr. Speaker, to try to convince the people in the east, if we have to use these words-and I deplore using the words "east" and "west" except geographically; and I hope that very soon that will be the only basis for using these words-of our sincerity in this matter.
Perhaps I may now continue with the quotation from the newspaper. This is from the Toronto Globe and Mail of recent date, June 29. It says:
"Quebeckers have no overriding authority to unify their thoughts; some may want one thing, while others something else'', he said.
That is referring to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). I said earlier that I had a great deal of respect for the minister who is

Canadian Flag
credited with uttering these words; but believe me, Mr. Speaker, when we have hon. members in this house on their feet time and time again repeating remarks such as I quoted earlier, it must be hard for the people of Quebec to understand what they do want. I want to put this on the record: I think the people of Quebec are the same kind of Canadians that I think I am, and the same kind of Canadians that I think we in the west are. I say again that I deplore this statement, "Two racial groups".
Hear, hear.
I want to conclude these remarks, Mr. Speaker, by referring to another matter.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker; could we hear about the flag issue?
Mr. Speaker, I only raise this point because this expression was used by an hon. member when speaking on the flag issue, and I am quoting from Hansard.
No; it was on the estimates.

If the hon. member will take the trouble to look it up, on page 4757 of Hansard he will see that the flag issue is referred to and this expression is used. The words used in Hansard are, "flag right now".
Before my time is concluded there are two other matters I want to bring to the attention of the house. At no time yet-and I hope there will come a time when we will hear more about this subject-have the wishes of a group of Canadians, who have never really been challenged as being real Canadians, been considered. I refer to the Indians, as we know them; treaty Indians, and some nontreaty Indians. I would like to pay tribute to them. I would also like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that probably my favourite constituent is a treaty Indian in the person of Senator James Gladstone of the other place.
Hear, hear.

I know that I hardly have the right to refer to the hon. gentleman in that way, but I am not doing so lightly, because the senator does live in my constituency and I do sincerely consider him to be my favourite constituent. I do not think there is any doubt about the fact that there is certainly nothing about race or creed or anything else connected with the Indians, so far as their recognition of a flag is concerned. What have they done about the ties with the
	*
past? There is one group that, perhaps the same as others, thinks we might use the totem pole as a Canadian symbol. There are others who think we might use an Indian headdress. There are those who would like to see a plain feather. But just lately a view among the Indians has more or less culminated in the opinion that we should use the symbol of the peace pipe. This suggestion came originally from the Six Nations Indians, who are very close to Ottawa as a matter of fact, and who have a very proud heritage. They consider themselves, even today, as allies of the Queen, even to the point where they do not too strongly consider Canada as a nation.
