Mr. Speaker, it is with great pride and pleasure that I come to add my modest contribution to that of the hon. members who spoke before me in this debate on the Canadian flag.
I am convinced that history will not forget the present debate and that we are now paving the way for our country's ultimate phase. We have reached the stage where we, in this house, as representatives of the Canadian people, are called upon to decide whether we have to live in the past, divide the nation as regards the present or head towards the future side by side. Several members emphasize the fact that many other bills should hold our attention and that the flag issue should be postponed.
I admit that the Canadian people are impatiently waiting for a great number of very important measures already appearing on the order paper. But we have only ourselves to blame if we do not make more progress in our work. Many of those pieces of legislation would have been passed by now if parliament were less interested in extending the debates and more anxious to achieve results.
If members of the house were to decide to postpone the selection of a flag, I suggest that it would not provide a solution to the problem, because failure of parliament to assume its responsibilities would be a failure to carry out the mandate conferred on it by the Canadian people.
The amendment under consideration this evening aims at relieving us from our obligations and relying on a plebiscite. It is not a very courageous solution. The mover of that resolution is apparently more interested in dividing than in legislating.
Mr. Speaker, our parliamentary system does not lend itself very well to a plebiscite. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has already pointed out, in his first speech on the flag, that there were only two plebiscites in Canadian history, one in 1898 on prohibition and the second in 1942 on conscription. And, as everyone knows, those two plebiscites have been failures.
Canadian Flag
Our parliamentary system is based, first, on the election of members whose duty it is to assume their own responsibilities. We have been entrusted with a mandate; we must act.
If a plebiscite were to be held on the flag issue, why should we not hold one with regard to pensions? Why not another one regarding franchise at 18? Why not another plebiscite on redistribution?
The suggestion of a plebiscite, in my opinion, is simply a putting-off, a smokescreen on the part of a leader who would like to cover up the divisions which rend his party as well as the indecisiveness which crippled him regarding the adoption of a flag.
Nonsense.

During the last two election campaigns, the party to which I am proud to belong promised to give Canada a distinctive flag within two years after taking office. We never pledged ourselves to hold a referendum on that question. Indeed, to my knowledge, no political party represented here stated during the election campaign that it would hold a referendum on the flag issue. In my opinion, that proposal is a last ditch effort, a desperate step to delay the adoption of a distinctive flag.
Yet, several hon. members claim that the red ensign which was given temporary approval in 1945, by virtue of an order in council, is a distinctive Canadian flag. I respect their opinion but I do not share it.
Everybody knows that the red ensign is the naval flag flown by all ships of the British merchant marine. It is the flag of various yachting clubs. It is the flag of many companies which have obtained their charters from the crown, such as perhaps the Hudson Bay Company. It also the flag of several colonies. In short, the red ensign is a respectable flag; it is also a respected flag. However, I do not think it a typical Canadian flag. It is a temporary flag which can be flown, as mentioned in the order in council of September 5, 1945:
-so long as parliament has not taken steps to adopt an official national flag.
Now, the time has come for parliament to adopt officially a typically distinctive flag.
If the history of the red ensign goes back officially to 1945 only, the three maple leaves on a single stem go back, as a heraldic symbol, to 1868. As a matter of fact, it is then that Queen Victoria gave as a symbol to Upper Canada-now Ontario-by royal decree, three gold maple leaves on a green field. That same 1868 decree gave as a

Canadian Flag
symbol to Lower Canada-which is Quebec today-three green maple leaves on a gold field.
Finally, on November 21, 1921, His Majesty George V, at the request of the Canadian Conservative government, promulgated red and white as the national colours of Canada and decreed as a Canadian emblem three maple leaves on a single stem.
Therefore, it seems a well established fact that the flag proposed in the resolution, that is three red maple leaves on a white field, is quite appropriate from the heraldic point of view and deeply faithful from the historic point of view. But if fondness for the past is a great virtue, a realistic approach to the present situation is also essential, and I would even say that for legislators and leaders, it is the future, much more than the past, which is important.
Mr. Speaker, I think I am right when I say that Canada is now going through one of the most distressing periods of its history.
I do not want to point out any further the extremist and vocal movements which stir the people in various places in the country. They already receive too much publicity.
But if those movements indicate a great unrest, they also reflect a national awakening.
It is our duty to direct those energies towards a positive goal, towards the unity of the nation. And a distinctive national flag as well as a constructive debate on this subject might inspire the Canadian people in a new national awakening and a total effort in order to achieve our potential and our aspirations.
Personally, I am convinced that the great majority of Canadians wish to preserve the Canadian nation and take part in the complete development of our economic and cultural assets.
Our country has a great future, and a really Canadian national flag may become the emblem of a new national pride and at the same time the starting point of a collective march towards our destiny.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Does the hon. member know that in 1961 his leader promised the Canadian people they would be told as to whether or not they wanted a certain distinctive national flag?
This is not the case at all. During two elections, the Liberal party promised the Canadian people a distinctive national flag. At no time was a referendum or a plebiscite promised or even mentioned.

May I ask another question? The hon. member was talking about a mandate. What was the mandate he received from constituents, or does this apply to all other constituencies? What was the mandate he received from his constituents?
The mandate was to carry out our program, and the flag is part of our program which we have to carry out within two years.
Did you tell them the program you were carrying out or the flag you were going to introduce?

Mr. Speaker, like many other members on all sides of the house I have been impressed, and considerably so, by the moderation which has been evident on the part of hon. members expressing their opinions during this debate. This bodes very well for the debate. It may seem unusual, but I should like to preface my remarks by a quotation from the leader of the New Democratic party, I might say a friend. I believe he has something the same background as I have. As I say, it may seem unusual that I would preface my remarks by quoting the remarks of that hon. member, but we have something in common, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) was raised in the industrial complex of the midlands of Scotland, while I was raised in the pastoral quietude of the borders. It stands to reason therefore that while we may have something in common, we may have our differences as well.
However, sir, if I may I should like to quote from the remarks of the hon. member which appear on page 4350 of Hansard:
The third thing I want to say something about, Mr. Speaker, is the actual design of the flag itself.
I have a good deal of sympathy for those who advocate selecting the red ensign, with some modifications, as the national flag of Canada. As one who was born in Scotland I have a deep attachment for British traditions and British institutions,
I would be very happy, personally, with a flag in which there was the union jack in one corner and the fleur-de-lis in another, thus paying tribute to the two great founding races that came together to make up the partnership of confederation.
This, Mr. Speaker, shows that those of us who had our background in the old land respond to these appeals to reason which

should typify all hon. members. I think in some respects the Prime Minister qualifies as one of those who have shown some restraint, because during the past month he has been appealing for moderation and a constructive approach to national unity. He says, of course, there are troublesome problems that must be solved and urges the peoples of the various cultures to show restraint. However, rather than restraint on the part of the government, there has been a certain amount of precipitate action to force an early decision on the flag issue, while matters of equal importance have been shelved for future consideration. Surely, sir, the Prime Minister could hardly intrude a more divisive issue into national debate at this time than the question of a new flag. Any attempt to erase ancient origins and traditions in the manner presently employed would inevitably touch off a situation that might split not only parliament but the nation as well.
A nation, even as young as Canada, can be proud of its Christian heritage, its honourable traditions which are presently embodied in our flag, and to fly a national emblem without those symbols of our historic background would be ignoring both the accomplishments of the past and the prospects for the future.
Flags may be as old as civilization, but they still retain much of their ancient power. Throughout history men have realized that they could express their feelings for their country and its people, their loyalty and sense of patriotic duty, by showing respect for their emblem, the national flag, and by understanding something of its meaning and its history. This helped them to be fellow citizens of a community instead of merely being people who happened to live together in one part of the earth. This is as true today as it ever was. We need not only respect our flags but protect them for posterity.
Over the years, designs on flags have not been picked at random or on the personal choice of one individual, but largely because of their meaning. Some have been deliberately selected in recent times, while others have been in use from time immemorial, their origins coming from ancient legends or being completely lost in the past. To interpret the meaning of a flag helps us to understand and appreciate something of the history and ideals of a country which flies it.
Obviously a flag of an innocuous pattern or an uninspiring design, such as is being presented for our consideration, fails to meet even the minimum standards which we should accept when judging it in comparison
Canadian Flag
with that which we have cherished in the past. It is for some of the reasons mentioned and, I may as well admit, for personal and sentimental reasons that I have on two occasions presented to the house a private member's bill for the adoption of the red ensign as Canada's national flag.
Naturally I have been impressed by the reasoning of other members who have spoken so eloquently on the government's proposed flag design and particularly by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), who I am sorry is not in the chamber tonight but who traced the use of the maple leaves as emblems and symbols as far back as 1862 and culminating, of course, in the extensive acceptance of the maple leaf insignia by our armed forces in world war II. However, in spite of the wide use of the maple leaf design the flag committee, which brought in its report in July of 1946, only saw fit to use the symbol as an integral part of the red ensign. This, of course, was in the days when we were spiritually uplifted, having made a great contribution to hostilities which were brought to a successful conclusion in 1945. Possibly in the report of the flag committee there was a projection of the public feeling which indicated a keener sense of the real values, exposed as our people had been to five years of war in which understanding, tolerance and sacrifice were present in greater measure than ever before as dominant features of human nature. I am not suggesting that those virtues are not present today, but in our present affluent and complacent society it does not seem that our vigour and determination are being properly applied if we accept this inadequate symbol as representing Canada's greatness today.
Should it happen that our present flag passes from the scene, there are those who will have deep and sincere misgivings as to what will be the next step in that path of retreat which will finally separate us from the commonwealth and the crown. If this is the view of only a small minority, then these apprehensions can only be dispelled by something more reassuring than the presentation of the present flag design. No action which will increase the divisions within the country at this time is justified, especially in view of the fact that those adversely affected have no way of making themselves heard except by representations through those who refuse to accept this form of dictation.
Like many other members I have had a great deal of correspondence regarding the flag issue over the past two years, possibly

Canadian Flag
because of the action I have taken in that regard. At the present tme my correspondence runs 90 per cent in favour of the red ensign. Strangely enough, many of those who have taken exception to the new flag proposal are not of my own political persuasion and find it difficult to have their own party members accept their opinions. Possibly this is one of the best reasons why we should support the reasoned appeal to rationalism which was proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Hamilton). Surely he proposed a reasonable idea which should be accepted. If the people of this country have an opportunity to voice their opinion, those who do not see eye to eye with the present proposal will gladly accept the will of the people of the rest of Canada. In conclusion may I say I am glad to support the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker).

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be able to take part for a few moments only, so as not to delay the proceedings, in the surely historical debate we are carrying on at present and to express my approval of resolution 44(A) introduced by this government.
Even though I must congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on his courage, such an issue must rise above any political allegiance. That is why I hold nothing against anyone and I do not defend any cause other than the unification of my country. We, as Canadians, should have a common ideal, regardless of our origin.
A flag is but a piece of material attached to a pole, but the important point at the present time is that it serves as an emblem, as a symbol, as a rallying sign. Accumulating or multiplying symbols serves no useful purpose.
It is difficult for me to understand why some members object to the formal adoption of a real national distinctive flag. May I labour this point.
When, in 1945, a ministerial decree recognized a flag for Canada, it is only accidentally and casually that it was proposed, and this flag was to remain until a distinctive official flag was adopted. It means, Mr. Speaker, that this possibility had been considered even by those who adopted temporarily the red ensign. This flag was not a distinctive and permanent national flag, and there was some hint of the possibility, which, today, is a fact, of permanently adopting some day an official, dis-

tractive, intrinsically Canadian flag, which no contingency could ever suppress.
I understand that this question requires sacrifices on both sides, especially for those who served so valiantly under such flag, since it is a highly emotional and sensitive question. It should not be forgotten that great things stemmed from sacrifice and self-denial; they were the more enduring if they required selfsacrifice. Let us work altogether in a gesture of harmony for the good of the country.
The time has come for us to produce a really distinctive flag, comprising no emblem belonging to another country. We have become an adult nation and we have to prove our maturity.
The essential thing should be now that this flag which is submitted to us receive official and absolute approval by statute, so as to be accepted in every part of this country and throughout our territory, without being left to local whims and prejudices. The approval of parliament which the Canadian people has been expecting for so long will, I trust, sanction a distinctive national flag, an official design consecrated by law. To us, it will be the exclusive symbol of Canada from sea to sea, and everywhere throughout the world.
I should not like to rehash all arguments in favour of the three maple leaves, and against a referendum which would only lead to as much confusion as if the 3,000 designs had been submitted to the house.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to state that I love my country, its people, of whatever origin and whatever political allegiance they may be. I have only one wish, and that is to see this country grow and prosper in harmony, in this diversity which can be held up as an example to the world, under a flag which would be truly and essentially Canadian for the benefit of Canada and all its citizens.

Mr. Speaker, if this catalogue of one's traditions is necessary, then I am going to indulge in it for a minute. It happens that in 1783 my paternal ancestors came from Connecticut to the part of Canada I happen to have the privilege of representing. Perhaps this labels me; it does according to some lights, anyway. My maternal ancestors came to Cape Breton from Scotland in the early part of the 19th century, but surely these facts in themselves -really they do not matter-do not make me British. Neither do they make me American; neither do they make me Scottish. I always look upon myself as a Canadian, and

to quote the immortal words of another in this house, "I am for Canada".
Having said that, however, I happen to be one of these naive people who believe in the universality of man. I would be delighted, for instance, if the United Nations flag could be adopted as the flag of Canada, and it might not be too bad a message for the world. Such a day is not now, I am realistic enough to know, but it must come I suggest in man's march toward a world order.
I also try to be realistic. I recognize and deeply appreciate the French fact in Canada. I sympathize with the aspirations of this cofounding race in its wish to take its rightful place in an evolving Canada. As a matter of fact, to show you how confused the whole issue is in Canada, and how careful a member of parliament must be in trying to articulate his beliefs, the other day when I made a comment in this house and used the phrase derisively about little Englanders in the sense that we in Canada, and any part of Canada, must not be isolationists, several of my constituents severely criticized me as being against England. So, a member of parliament is in great difficulty and has to take great care.
I happen to support a distinctive Canadian flag, but having said that I think it is fair to say that distinctive means different things to different people. The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Dube), who has spoken and who represents a part of New Brunswick, felt that distinctive means the ignoring of our past, using the word in the sense that everything that went before in our land must be turned aside. But to me the word distinctive means something different from that. It means something unique, something special, something which stands by itself.
I happen to believe that a flag which embodies the union jack and the fleur-de-lis, or any other symbol acceptable to the French, or recognition of the French partnership in Canada's growth and development, would mean and be a distinctive Canadian flag. For weeks now, although this debate has only been going on for three days, I have been hearing derisive things said about those loyal Canadians whose entire background and tradition make it perfectly obvious they would wish to honour and revere the red ensign. These Canadians have been taught to do this in their schools. They have even been admonished to do so by those who in earlier days- and not so very long ago at that-sat in the seats now occupied by the Prime Minister
Canadian Flag
and his colleagues and, as a matter of fact, led and supported the party which the Prime Minister now leads and supports. My allusion here is of course to Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King.
It seems fairly obvious that there should not be a grade or a degree of patriotism or, as some use the word, of Canadianism in our land. No one has a monopoly on patriotism or upon feelings of loyalty to this country and its institutions.
I am not here today to swear allegiance or to put my love of country to any test. Everything right and good and true does not repose in the breast of the Prime Minister or in the breasts of those who support him. Everything wrong and out of date and disloyal does not rest in the being of my leader and those of my colleagues who have taken strong positions on what I call this manufactured issue.
I have a formula-it is not new but I want to present it-for trying to resolve this so-called flag issue, and I propose to strip it of all complications and complexities. At least it has been stripped in my mind and, if I am any good at all, I will be able to present it to the house in a fairly clear way. My formula would give each Canadian eligible to vote a share in the determination of the distinctive Canadian flag.
I support the proposal of my leader for a referendum or plebiscite. I suggest that the people should share in this momentous decision we are about to take. Our flag, as has been said before, must not be allowed to become a Pearson flag. Our flag must not be allowed to become a Liberal flag-with the large L of that much maligned word. Our flag must not become-as it may be, unless we take a very close checkrein on our emotions -a partisan flag. Rather, it seems to me to be obvious that a flag should be one the final choice of which is shared by the greatest possible number of Canadians. Some members who have spoken from the other side talk about a mandate. It is obvious to the country and it is certainly obvious to anyone in this house that there is no such thing as a clear and decisive mandate on this issue. This is, in the immortal words of the leader of the Social Credit party, a house of minorities, and I do not see how in any house of minorities on an issue which transcends partisan aspects and goes to the roots of people's traditions and beliefs, the government can properly claim that it holds a mandate for making this change in the manner in which they propose to make it. I suggest the people

Canadian Flag
should be allowed to decide and I think this simple, honest and practical act on the part of the Prime Minister would immediately dispel any suspicion, if there is any suspicion, of partisanship in the consideration of this issue. Let the people decide, and all division will wither away because a democratic process would have been followed. Let the people decide, and obviously we will have a flag which the majority have selected in the way I am about to indicate as being their preference.
The hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska (Mr. Dube) and no doubt others who have spoken, have referred to the two other plebiscites, the plebiscite on prohibition, which was a failure, and the plebiscite in 1942. I wonder where the blame should properly lie for the failure of those two plebiscites. The blame in 1942 seems to be reasonably obvious. History can tell us that. And if anybody is interested in the plebiscite on prohibition I suppose I could give a learned dissertation on it. But perhaps the following might be recommended to the people of Canada for a decision on the basis of a first, second, third, fourth and fifth choice, listed in whatever order the house would prefer. I happen to have listed them in the order I intend to give now:
1.	Whether a distinctive Canadian flag should be the red ensign as presently constituted;
2.	the three maple leaf design suggested in the resolution before us;
3.	the single maple leaf design recommended by the New Democratic party;
4.	the triangle design incorporating a single maple leaf, suggested I understand by the Saint Jean Baptiste society, or
5.	an adaptation of the red ensign so as to include a fleur de lis or a maple leaf or any other symbol in the fly, rather than the great seal of Canada which is now in the red ensign.
This formula of choice would, it seems to me, present a fair series with a wide aspect of selection to the people of Canada. The people could indicate their preference in a democratic way by numbering their various choices in accordance with their wishes. By this formula, the final solution will be the result of the efforts of everybody in this country who took the trouble to make a choice at all.
While Canadians were making their choice and the results were being tabulated, it seems to me this parliament could go about its

urgent business. We have had some indication from the Prime Minister in his statement this evening of the issues the government thinks -and I share this opinion-are urgent. But this is after all a mediocre list-a list of expediencies. It is a list which does not include in any way the fundamental and ongoing problems of this country. By this suggestion of mine Canadians would be given a choice according to their preferences and we would not be subjected here to the game of hide and seek caused by the government's other items to which, understandably, it wishes to give priority.
Another thing which could be dispelled by this formula of mine would be the overriding threat of a general election which seems to be put forward by the Prime Minister and other members of the government every time somebody wants to take a rightful share in the debates in this house. These threats are born of frustration because of bad organization, and I think they are to be repudiated by people who have tried to explain the proper function of a free and democratic parliament. We have had a new gimmick tonight in this faltering endeavour to bring some semblance of order to a perambulating parliament. I suggest that the Prime Minister has advanced the threat of closure on this issue in every aspect but that of the actual rules. I suggest his statement about the disposal of this flag resolution amounts to de facto closure.
Now I see it is 10.30 and everybody will wish to ponder my words over the next 48 hours.

subtopic: TRAIL, B.C.-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO OVERTIME MAIL DELIVERY
TRAIL, B.C.-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO OVERTIME MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for appearing so frequently on this late night show, but duty impels me. A few days ago I received a telegram from Robert Keiver, president of local 480 of the Trail and district smelter workers union. I will read the telegram:
This is to advise you that commencing at about 7 p.m. Monday June twenty second a special delivery of mail was made door to door to Trail members of our union. Normally no mail delivery is scheduled for this time of day. Our information is and can be attested to that postal employees at Trail were requested at about 2 p.m. to work overtime for four hours after 6 p.m. These postal employees were obliged to make a delivery over and above normal deliveries which consisted mainly of a communication from the employer Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company to each of its employees residing in the city of Trail in company envelopes and metered indicating four cent postage rate. This extraordinary privilege accorded by the Post Office Department to Cominco takes place on the eve of a referendum being conducted by the union representing the employees and the vote is a phase of a labour dispute between the company and its employees. We are not objecting to the content of the material distributed in this instance but seriously question the principle involved which appears designed to give an employer an advantage in a dispute with his employees. We respectfully request you to raise this matter and demand a full investigation by the responsible federal authorities.
That is signed, "R. Keiver, president, local 480, Trail and district smelter workers". Mr. Speaker, I have also received other telegrams and several 'phone calls from interested persons in the district. This has created quite a lot of comment in the district, because it is considered a somewhat unusual circumstance. I have been informed that some of the postmen at least were in uniform when they were delivering these special delivery letters. I have been reliably informed that only four cents postage was paid by Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company instead of the 29 cents that is normally required under the circumstances. I have been informed recently that the postmen are not certain, even at this date, whether they will be paid by Consolidated
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Mining and Smelting Company for this overtime or by the Post Office Department.
On that account, Mr. Speaker, I asked the minister the following question a few days ago:
Has the minister any information to give the house with respect to his inquiries concerning an unconventional special delivery of mail in Trail, undertaken at the request of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Co. Ltd. on the evening prior to a vote of the employees on an arbitration award?
We all know the minister has an excellent record as a good administrator and in wartime he rendered good service to his country in this respect; and he has an excellent record since in British Columbia in his association with the forestry industry. I am sure, therefore, he wants everything in his department to be run according to Hoyle and according to the regulations. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, because of the concern of the union men concerned and other patrons of the Trail post office, and in view of the apparent irregularities, I would appreciate it very much if the minister would give the house some information with respect to what appears to be a most unusual situation.

subtopic: TRAIL, B.C.-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO OVERTIME MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having furnished me with a copy of the telegram in question and a subsequent telegram which he received. Within a matter of minutes of the time I received the first wire I gave instructions to look into this matter. We received a preliminary report by telephone. It was not complete. Because I was going to be in the west over the week end I assured my hon. friend that I would make inquiries while there and would let him and the house have a further report today.
I have little to add to what the hon. member has said. The letters in question, and there were many of them, were delivered at the post office in Trail in the late afternoon of the day in question. They were stamped, as the hon. member says, with a four-cent stamp, or rather they were metered with a four-cent stamp charge recorded. I do want to make perfectly clear that if there is any fault in the matter the fault is not that of the postmaster in Trail.
After the letters were delivered to the post office a request came from the company to deliver the letters during the evening; at least, an inquiry was made as to whether they could be delivered during the evening. The company said they were prepared to pay any reasonable charge for this extra work. A rate

Answer to Question
was suggested for the postmen who might be willing to deliver these letters during the evening. The postmaster then quite properly called his superior in Vancouver, the district director. By this time it was evening and the district director, thinking he had a precedent for so doing, because of the time factor, authorized the postmaster in Trail to put the proposition to the postmen and ask them whether or not they would be willing to deliver the letters that evening at the rate of so much per hour. It was not a request but an inquiry. All but one of them said they would take the advantage of the opportunity to make some overtime. They showed up in the early evening at the post office, some in uniform and some not, and they delivered the letters.
In the course of my conversation I asked the district director to produce the file on which he relied as a precedent. That file has not yet been supplied to me; he undertook to send it off by air mail either last night or today. I agree with the hon. member that there seems to have been an irregularity, to say the least. The district director gave me to understand they would have done the same thing for the union, although that does not excuse
it if it is improper. When I receive the report, which I would expect to receive, not tomorrow because of the holiday but on Thursday, I will advise my hon. friend further. I also intend to have a legal opinion on the position and if disciplinary action is required in the case of the district director it will be taken. But until I see the documents on which he relied as a precedent I cannot definitely say that there has been a breach of the regulations.
It is certainly an extraordinary procedure, one which should not be encouraged, and I must say I commend the district director for saying frankly: "If anyone is responsible, I am; don't blame the postmaster". As I say, I will keep the hon. member informed, and if further action needs to be taken I can assure him it will be taken.
